subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, August 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pickers-gill for the second reading of Bill No. 439, to amend the Indian Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill has already had considerable discussion on the resolution stage and the minister has made a fairly extensive statement on the motion for second reading, so it should not be necessary to cover a lot of ground at this point. I would like to make it clear at once that we are opposed to the second reading of this bill because we do not consider that it meets the desires of the Indians or the requirements of the situation. There are three main grounds on which we think the bill falls short of what is desirable.
The first of these is with respect to its handling of the liquor situation in so far as the rights of Indians to obtain liquor are concerned. Our objection here in the main is that the dominion government appears to be avoiding its responsibility for a decision as to whether or not the franchise with respect to liquor should be extended to Indians. I have read carefully the minister's statement as reported at page 6408 of Hansard, and I refer particularly to the passage reading:
We are providing for a provincial initiative which would make it possible for the Indians in
[Mr. Blackmore.l
a province to be brought under all the liquor laws of the province, but the initiative would have to be taken by the provincial government.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to misrepresent the situation. That is only one of two alternatives.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. I shall now complete the paragraph in order that there will be no suggestion of unfairness. I continue:
There is this further proviso, that any band which by a majority of its membership decides not to come under the general law could establish a form of local option on the reserve.
The minister went on to mention this second proposal which would allow the band on a particular reserve to take the initiative. We realize, of course, that there must be consultation with the provincial governments because I think without exception the provincial governments have liquor legislation of their own laying down the circumstances under which residents of the province may obtain liquor.
I am not suggesting for a moment that the dominion government should pass legislation with respect to the right of access of Indians to liquor without consultation with the provinces, but we do suggest that this government must accept the responsibility, without seeking to pass it on or evade it, for deciding whether or not Indians are to have access to liquor. Once having made that decision then of course it must be implemented, whichever is the decision, in a manner agreeable to the provinces. But we do not consider it is sound in principle that while Indians are the wards and responsibility of the government of the Dominion of Canada, the main responsibility for the decision as to whether or not they should have the right of access to liquor should be passed on to some other government. For that reason we think the provision in the present legislation is undesirable.
The second main ground of criticism of the legislation is that once again the government has allowed the opportunity to pass for making provision for appeals by Indians from decisions of the minister or of the governor in council affecting Indian rights. This is a matter to which the Indians attach a great deal of importance. Indian associations, as well as associations of white persons having particular interest in Indian welfare all across Canada, have for years been urging that the act should be amended to provide that where a decision is made which affects an Indian with respect to his status as an Indian or which affects an Indian with respect to his

right to or interest in property on the reserve, whether it be real or personal, that decision should be subject to the right of appeal to the courts of the land.
In the past we have expressed our agreement with the principle now sought to be followed by the department, that is that Indians should gradually be brought to a level where they are admitted to citizenship. This is an educational process; this is a gradual process. One of the most outstanding fields in which Indians do not as yet have the same rights as white citizens is this question of the right of access to the courts. It does seem to us to be contradictory to the principle which the department states it is following to continue to deny to Indians that right of appeal.
Reference was made in the discussion on the resolution stage to a submission by the Indian association of Alberta dated January, 1956. I think special importance should be attached to this submission. The submission was thoroughly reviewed by a solicitor who acts in the capacity of friend and adviser to this association and to the Indians. This is a well-considered and well-reasoned brief, one of the opening passages of which is as follows:
We are strongly advised also to work to get this appeal clause added.
"In any section of the Indian Act where the minister's discretion or that of the governor in council is exercised in any manner which an Indian or band of Indians feels is inequitable, there shall be an appeal from that decision to a judge of the supreme court of the province where the Indian or band of Indians is located."
There has been widespread support for that principle. It is not, however, incorporated in the bill. The bill leaves unchanged the present situation, which denies Indians the right of access to courts. When changes as extensive as these are being made in the Indian Act we believe this one should also be included, and for that reason we intend to move an appropriate amendment in the committee stage.
I should also mention something that I omitted to say when dealing with the question of liquor and the way in which it is dealt with under the bill. This same Indian association of Alberta has made a very critical finding with respect to that matter. In paragraph 5 they say, with regard to the general question of liquor and the effect of the present legislation:
The Indian association of Alberta has asked good legal advice on this. We are told that Ottawa is now asking the Indians to break this rule. Ottawa is not willing to run the risk of doing its own breaking. You are being given the chance to do it against yourselves. Are you willing to start breaking the treaty?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Could the hon. gentleman give the date of that submission?
Indian Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: It is dated January, 1956.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: That is long before anybody had ever seen the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
One of the criticisms we have heard and to which I was intending to refer in concluding is that there had not been adequate consultation with the Indians themselves as to the effect of the legislation and as to its contents, and what the minister has said seems to me to indicate that this is a well founded criticism.
The third ground on which we criticize the bill is that in many cases the act is being changed to provide that whereas formerly decisions affecting Indians were to be taken by the governor in council, they are now to be made by ministerial order. This subject was discussed in some detail by the minister last night, and he presented us an interesting summary of his views and of the history of the situation, the effect of which was that there are so many matters of small administrative detail that come before cabinet for decision that unless there is some review of the whole situation made and a conscious attempt to cut down on the number of decisions required by order in council, then in effect the administrative machinery of cabinet will bog down in a welter of detail.
It may well be that there is very real substance to what the minister has said, but with one item I was not particularly impressed: the argument about the time necessary to deal with this mass of orders in council. The minister read us a very interesting and very sound memorandum, it seemed to me, by Sir George Murray, based on a study he made in 1912, and he pointed out the growth in the number of orders in council since that day. I hope the minister will permit me to point out to him that the answer might also be advanced that the salaries of cabinet ministers have also been considerably increased since that day.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: The number of hours in a day has not.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
These gentlemen accept gladly the office to which they are called. Whilst no one would want them to carry on in a manner which is bound to be inefficient, it seems to me that the argument of the hardship imposed on ministers is perhaps not the strongest argument that could be advanced. The minister himself referred to the situation regarding treasury board. Many of those decisions which previously had to be taken by the full cabinet are now taken by treasury board, which is in effect a committee of cabinet.
This of course is a very sound administrative procedure. If it is found in fact that

Indian Act
the volume of orders in council is such that it is just not physically possible to deal with them in full cabinet, why not enlarge the system which resulted in the establishment of treasury board and have a committee of cabinet so that a committee, of whatever size might be convenient, would review the recommendation which must, of course, come first from the department, from the minister concerned, and if the committee were satisfied that the recommendation was sound it would then so report to the full cabinet, with the result that when these orders in council came before the cabinet the main question to be asked would be: Does the committee approve? If the committee approved, then I fancy it would follow automatically that the cabinet as a whole would approve the order in council.
But, sir, I realize that one who has had any firsthand knowledge of the problems of the cabinet must, in fairness, accept the word of the minister that this is a very real problem and that it is time that some serious consideration was given to it. I believe the suggestion I have just made would be one way of meeting it, at least partly. Whether or not the suggestion is sound, we believe that the Indian Act is the wrong act to begin with, the wrong act with which to start to take away responsibility for decisions from the governor in council and vest it in the minister.
The Indians are in a unique position, and this is probably true not only in Canada but throughout the world, in that they are the responsibility, the wards of the dominion government. Their whole situation and welfare, to a degree not equalled in any way by the white citizens of this country, are dependent upon the policy and administrative decisions taken by the government, and in many respects they are unable to defend themselves against injustices, real or fancied, which follow from those decisions.
Therefore I believe it is only proper to suggest, since the decisions made have a unique significance in their bearing on the welfare of the Indians who are the responsibility of the government, that these decisions be made and the responsibility for them be accepted in name as well as in fact by the governor in council, that is the government as a whole, instead of by one minister. This is a matter to which again the Indians attach particular importance, and if we are trying to gain their confidence, trust and respect in the efforts being made to bring them up gradually to full citizenship, then it does seem to me that it would be a seriously mistaken policy at one fell swoop and in an amendment to the Indian Act of this sort to provide against 
their own expressed wishes that these decisions shall be made at the ministerial level instead of at the level of the governor in council.
That is not the way to gain the confidence of the Indians. However inconvenient it might be, we submit in all seriousness that from the point of view of the larger interest and the larger picture the government should accept that inconvenience because of the good results which will flow in building up mutual trust, respect and confidence between the government and the Indians.
To summarize, we believe that provision for decision on Indian matters by the cabinet should be retained and that the additional step should be taken toward the equalization of the position of the Indians and white citizens of giving the Indians the right of appeal to the courts of this country from such executive decisions. Because the act does not meet these requirements and because in our view it seeks to impose on provincial governments a responsibility for decision with regard to the liquor question so far as the Indians are concerned, we intend to oppose the bill on second reading.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night the minister went into a lot of history dealing with orders in council, orders of the treasury board and going away back to 1912 when Sir Kobert Borden's government was in power. I do not know whether that was for the benefit of the hon. member for Kamloops or for whose benefit it was. However, the way in which the minister rattled off dates and data showed that he knew history, anyway.
What I should be interested in hearing from the minister is what progress his department has made in implementing the recommendations of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons relating to the Indian Act which were tabled on June 22, 1948. Mr. Speaker, you will remember that some of the recommendations-and I am going to mention a few of them-had to do with treaty rights and obligations. At that time the committee found that there was great difficulty in letting the Indians know that they were asking for things that could not possibly be given to them. I remember that at that time the hon. member for Lethbridge was a strong supporter of a clause that was incorporated in the report. I shall read it to you, as follows:
1. Treaty rights and obligations.
Your committee recommends that a commission in the nature of a claims commission be set up, with the least possible delay, to inquire into the terms of all Indian treaties in order to discover and determine, definitely and finally, such rights and obligations as are therein involved and.

Indian Act
further, to assess and settle finally and in a just and equitable manner all claims or grievances which have arisen thereunder.
I want the minister to look up these things again. I will not read them all, but there is one I should like to mention. With an election coming up, most hon. members will be interested in it. I refer to clause 5, which reads as follows:
5. Eligibility of Indians to vote at dominion elections.
As part of the education and preparation of the Indian to assume his place in the Canadian body politic, your committee recommend, on May 6 last, that "voting privileges for the purpose of dominion elections be granted to Indians on the same status as electors in urban centres". This is a matter which, in the opinion of your committee, should be referred to a special committee on the dominion elections act, with a view to early implementation of the recommendation.
It is realized that many Indians are not anxious to have or to use the franchise, under the misapprehension that, if they do exercise it, they will lose what they considered their rights and privileges.
Many Indians who do not have the right to vote at dominion elections do pay taxes on income earned away from the reserve, together with sales tax, gasoline tax, excise tax, et cetera. This is taxation without representation.
It is the opinion of your committee that it would encourage Indians, particularly the younger ones, to interest themselves in public affairs, if they were given the privilege already recommended Your committee is further of opinion that the public generally would be given a better appreciation of Indian affairs.
I have only one more recommendation that I am going to read, and it deals with the bill more specifically than anything else that I can see. I refer to clauses 9 and 10:
9. Indian administration in general.
In 1946 and again in 1947 the joint committee on the Indian Act made recommendations with regard to administrative improvements which could be effected without the revision of existing legislation and which, when put into effect, would remove some of the causes out of which arise grievances and complaints of many Indians.
There are still some "administrative improvements" which your committee deems advisable.
Your committee, therefore, again recommends that the administration of all aspects of Indian affairs be placed under one ministerial head.
Your committee reiterates the recommendation maae by the 1947 joint committee on the Indian Act, viz:
10 The director of the Indian affairs branch should be named a commissioner who shall have the rank of a deputy minister and shall have at least two assistant commissioners of whom one should be a Canadian of Indian descent.
I should like to go a little further with this, but it is so close to the end of the session that if you make a speech of any length you are apt to be frowned upon by your colleagues. I have quoted these three recommendations, and I want the minister to look into the matter and see just how far we have gone to meet the recommendations 67509-452i
of the committee. The committee sat for three years and held over 100 meetings. It was a large committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one matter that I should like to refer to. In this bill some change has been made respecting the use of liquor on Indian reserves and the use of liquor by Indians. I notice that by the legislation responsibility is now passed over to the provinces. The provinces enact that they are going to allow the Indians to use liquor under the provincial laws, and the bands decide they are going to allow liquor to be used on the Indian reserves, if it conforms with the provincial law. It seems to me that is a negation of the responsibility of the federal government in this respect, and I think it should be very carefully watched.
The federal government, operating under the Indian Act, undertakes to care for these people, the Indians of North America, who are basically a very fine people. Where are they today? They have degenerated during the white man's occupation of this part of the continent to a position where I do not think we can look with very much pride on their present status. However, I would say that in the past 15 years there has been some change in the attitude of the government and some change in the attitude of the people generally.
These people have very few rights; they have very little power of appeal. They surrendered this land under treaties which were signed in good faith from time to time by the representatives of the Indian groups with the representatives of Queen Victoria. In some of those treaties they asked to be protected against the evil influences of liquor.
In the treaties signed by the representatives of the Queen the government promised to take care of them and to see that they were not hurt by the evil influences of the white man's drink. It seems to me that in the present legislation the government, which is responsible for the administration

Indian Act
of Indian affairs, is passing that responsibility over to the provincial governments. Have the provincial governments any responsibility under the Indian treaties, or are those the responsibilities of the federal government?
From my study of the Indian Act, and from my watching of the administration of it, it seems to me one very salient point emerges; that is that the terms of the treaties are forgotten almost entirely and the rights of Indians under the treaties are not being fully recognized. The trend toward the recognition of their rights, or at any rate living up to the spirit of those treaties, is something that we should watch very carefully. When I look at what Canada has done for her Indians and compare it with what New Zealand has done for her Maori people it seems to me we have neglected those people far too much.
The conditions of health among those people have been very bad over the years. Recently, under the Department of National Health and Welfare, there has been a fine improvement in the tuberculosis rate, but economically in many parts of the country the Indians are in a very poor condition. [DOT]Certainly they are in no position to make very much progress. I know that is true so far as the education and training of those 'people are concerned. How can the Indian in this country, in the economic conditions under which he is forced to live on many of the reserves, possibly become a Canadian citizen? How can he advance?
The training of the Indian is of the utmost importance. In far too many instances the Indian is trained in the residential schools in such a way that he is not satisfied to go back and live on his reserve in the condition in which his parents lived. He is not trained to go out in the white man's world and make his living among white men. He is lost between two worlds when he comes out of school in the formative period of his life. He is unfit and untrained to take his place. So long as those conditions exist the Indians as a race and as a people cannot advance.
I believe the administration responsible for the care of those people should make basic changes in their education and training. My first suggestion would be that the basis of their economic life should be made sound so they can live. My second suggestion would be to make available to them educational facilities in line with their abilities to assimilate, and train them for the particular life which they are going to have to live and make it possible for them to advance as a race.
These people have done well in the roles they have played in our wars. The young
[Mr. Castleden.l
men who enlisted in the armed forces and received medical care, proper food and proper training, advanced tremendously. They are people of tremendous ability; they are people of very fine basic principles of religious life. The Indian believes that he should love and help his fellow man and look upon one another as brothers. I do suggest that under the act the minister should be careful to see that all the things that were promised to the Indians in their original treaties are fulfilled, and that they are not being violated by this legislation which passes over the responsibility for granting the right to use liquor on the reserves to the provincial governments, which certainly have signed no treaty and certainly have no responsibility in that regard.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the province of British Columbia we have had for the past several years a provincial advisory committee on Indian Affairs which has been doing admirable work. I have the 1955 report of this committee, and there are two observations on the very first page. The first is that during the past year there has been evidence of increasing interest on the part of the public relative to the conditions under which our Indian friends are living at the present time.
The other observation is that there is an awakening sense of responsible leadership among the Indians themselves which, in different communities, is prompting them to take a more vital part in the industrial and community life of the particular province in which this committee is working. I believe this is very significant, because sometimes we wonder just what the response of the Indian people may be to the efforts which are put forth on their behalf. There are some who think there is little appreciation of the efforts put forth. I am afraid some feel that little is accomplished, at least of a permanent nature. This committee does feel, however, that there is a very splendid response by the Indian people themselves to the efforts being put forth on their behalf.
As far as education is concerned, the young people are taking their places in the educational institutions of our province. A great many of them are now attending public schools, and they fit in very well with the life in those schools. Not only that, but with regard to vocational and apprenticeship training we find there is an increasing interest in this particular field. As a result of the provincial advisory committee's recommendations regarding vocational and apprenticeship training the director of apprenticeship has given thought to means by which

these Indians can be encouraged to take part to a greater extent in these activities.
A three-point program has been drawn up. First the Indian young people must be selected and training provided for them free of cost. Second, employment should be found for them and a close liaison maintained during the first year or so of their employment. Third, vocational training programs should be provided for them during each year of their apprenticeship until their training is completed.
In the second annual report dealing with public relations there is a brief paragraph to which I would like to call attention. It reads as follows:
Allied to the rising Indian population in this province is the fact that an increasing number of Indians are seeking integration into the social and industrial life of British Columbia. This move by the Indians toward the white man's way of life is placing a responsibility upon the rest of the inhabitants of this province to encourage and assist the process of integration.
I believe it is the desire and intention of the minister and his department to give assistance in every way possible to this particular movement, to encourage our Indian friends to integrate into community projects and in every way to encourage them to endeavour to take their place as citizens of this great country of ours.
There have been objections raised relative to the bill presently before us. I believe the hon. member for Prince Albert, speaking at the resolution stage, made the suggestion that this resolution was premature because of the fact that sufficient study had not been given to all the problems relating to Indian affairs and provisions were not made for remedial action in this particular measure.
I do not think we ought to wait until we have a perfect measure to discuss and pass, because if that were so I do not think we would ever do anything in this connection. There is a great difference of opinion even among the Indians themselves relative to what they want and what would be in the best interests of their people. There is also a wide variety of opinion among other citizens of Canada relative to the same matter, and if we are going to wait until we have something that is absolutely perfect then I suggest we will not have anything at any time.
I feel, therefore, that this legislation, despite the fact that there may be inadequacies and omissions as far as desirable features are concerned, is deserving of our support. Although there are many things we could criticize about it, I feel this legislation makes some headway. We are endeavouring to face the problem and find a solution for it, and
Indian Act
because we feel it is an improvement and a step in the right direction we intend to give it our support. The very fact that additional funds are being provided for loans is in itself a very admirable feature, and therefore we are going to support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but view some of the clauses of this bill with apprehension, particularly the one relating to liquor for Indians. The idea of turning over decisions on this matter to the provincial authorities, in the matter of delegating power and authority to the provinces to act with regard to liquor permits for Indians, strikes me as a rather retrograde step.
If one delegates one's power and authority to others and they take certain actions which one does not like, one finds oneself in the position of a minister who leaves it to some of his personnel to decide policy matters. The minister is then in the position of having to support the policy established by his officials. I think we may find ourselves in that position if we delegate the authority for allowing or disallowing liquor on Indian reserves to the provincial authorities.
Throughout history we as a federal government have had complete charge of Indians and their affairs, and I think a departure from that policy and the acceptance of a course of action which would delegate that authority to someone else is questionable, to say the least. Certainly we all know the effect of liquor on Indians.

The majority of complaints that have been made to me from time to time concerning the conduct of Indians under the

Indian Act
influence of alcohol indicate that these occurrences develop when there has been a relaxing of R.C.M.P. supervision in the particular area. I recall one incident when the R.C.M.P. office was closed and relocated several miles away. The immediate result was that the Indians on the reserves located nearby the former R.C.M.P. post went more or less berserk. It was practically impossible for women to walk down the streets of those little towns at night. I made representations to the Department of Justice and my good friend the minister of that department took remedial action. The R.C.M.P. were put back in supervision in that area, and the situation was cleared up.
Once you remove this supervision the problems increase. Perhaps I do not understand this bill correctly, and I hope in his explanatory remarks the minister will deal with these points. I am not at all satisfied that this is not a retrograde step so far as the control of Indians is concerned. I think we are going to put the R.C.M.P. in a position where it is much harder for them to control the situation than it is now. I think I have said enough on that point.
When the minister is explaining this to the house I hope he will touch upon the matter of family allowances as it is handled here. I believe there is something in the *changes in this act which may amount to a change in the concept of the family allowance; that is, it has now become a premium for staying away from school. There has been some indication in my riding that they consider it a paying proposition as far as half-breed children are concerned to stay home. It must be remembered that it is hard to tell a half-breed child from an Indian child because the line of demarcation is so fine. In some families you will find two full brothers, one of whom is considered to be a half-breed and the other, considered to be an Indian.
Having had this unhappy example of children being able to stay away from school in order to get family allowances, I hope there will be something in this bill to make sure that Indian children go to school. Otherwise we are going to have many schools in my area rapidly becoming surplus. They are not too happy about going to school in the first place, and it is only such things as family allowances directed in a manner so as to act as an incentive for school attendance, that we can get these children to go to school. The missions in the north have had a tremendous influence in getting these people to take up education. They have finally reached the point where they realize

that they cannot subsist off the resources of the land and must seek other employment.
With these two reservations I shall wait for the minister's explanation. I hope he will be able to satisfy me on these two points; otherwise I shall have to vote against this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up very much time but there are one or two things I should like to deal with. When the hon. member for Meadow Lake was dealing with the question of liquor I thought at first I would be in complete agreement with him. I think it is a rather dubious principle that we should have the implementation of certain parts of this act in the hands of provincial legislatures. After all, these provisions with regard to liquor do in some measure alter the status of the Indian as a Canadian citizen, and that is a responsibility which should be retained by this house.
I imagine that in my own province of British Columbia it may not make much difference, for the obvious reason that the Indians have a provincial vote and therefore the provincial government will base their action upon the wishes of their Indian citizens. I think the minister could well reconsider that particular provision. I intend to deal with it when we are in the committee stage.
There is another matter which I feel should have some study, and that is the question of the position of the Indian when enfranchised. As I have said, I realize it is extremely difficult to legislate for people with such a wide variety of development as the Indians in British Columbia. When I hear comments such as those made by the hon. member for Meadow Lake-I am quite sure he was quite sincerely reporting conditions as he had heard of them or seen them in his own area-I realize that they are quite ludicrously inapplicable to the Indians with whom I come in contact. Those Indians are advancing very rapidly, and I think that has been recognized. I believe in the next few years we will have to go much further than this bill. Therefore I am not too much concerned about the shortcomings I see in it or its inadequacy, because I believe with the rapid advancement of the Indian people we are probably going to have to amend this act almost every other year.
I am not too much concerned over the point raised by the hon. member for Kamloops with regard to the ostensible transfer of powers from the governor in council to the minister. I would not want the minister to take this as indicating unbounded confidence in him as minister, but I strongly

suspect that this is merely putting in legal form what actually takes place at the present time. I suspect that probably the governor in council does not examine too closely the recommendations of this minister or of other ministers when they come before council, and that what we are doing now is placing the responsibility upon the person who actually makes the decision. Of course in the final analysis the cabinet as a whole is responsible for the actions of any minister. I can see how this would step up the administrative work of the department, so for that reason, and I think I can speak for all my colleagues, I intend to support this measure as it is. We shall have some detailed criticism when it comes before the committee of the whole.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I happen to represent a riding in which an Indian band is located, and I am happy to be able to say that those Indians seem to be of a much higher calibre than the Indians referred by the hon. member for Meadow Lake. Indians from the Rama reserve have filled some important positions and portfolios within the boundaries of Canada in professional fields. They enlisted to a man in both the first and second world wars. Many of them brought back wives from Scotland and England and other parts of Europe. They live on the reserve and are considered as full-blooded Indians.
As far as those Indians are concerned I submit that they have the right to full Canadian citizenship, and that should be given to them as soon as legislation in that respect can be passed. We did not worry about them having the right to enter a beer parlor or to purchase liquor when they were enlisting in the Canadian army in both wars. For a short period I served with some of those Indians and they were not any worse so far as liquor was concerned than other Canadian soldiers. They were good soldiers and brave men.
I submit that this government should assume its responsibility and bring these Indians to full Canadian citizenship. They should have the vote. Before bringing in a bill of this kind the government and the minister and the department should have talked it over with the Indians to see what they would like to have. I feel that my Indians are quite capable of passing on legislation in their own behalf.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to cover briefly all the points raised this morning, and I should like to start by referring to the speech made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, because I find myself in
Indian Act
agreement with everything he said. I echo his approbation of the work of the provincial advisory committee of British Columbia. I should like to say one thing which perhaps may be regarded as an interference in the provincial field. We have found in the Indian affairs branch that as soon as Indians are given the vote provincially their situation improves. This has been most marked in British Columbia in the way of increased public interest, as the hon. member has said.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: In Ontario, too.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
As the hon. member said also, there has been an increased and awakening sense of Indian leadership. I echo what the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) has just said. I happen to know quite well, I think, one of the people he has in mind, and I would say there is no finer citizen of Canada, if we are thinking of the same person.
With the hon. member for Selkirk I think the beginning of what has been a new orientation for the Indian population began with that joint committee on which, I believe, he served. I shall try, when my estimates come up, to say something about the progress made in carrying out some of those recommendations. I do not think I shall attempt today to say anything about giving the federal franchise to Indians generally. That is not provided in this bill. That is a subject that has some difficulties, for two reasons. In the first place, many of the Indians are still suspicious of it as a device to take away something they now have, and I think we must make sure that we disabuse most of them of that idea before we take this step.
There is also the fact-I have expressed this very frankly to the Indians, and I want to say the same thing in this house-that taxation without representation is certainly repugnant to us, and I think that representation without equality in taxation is also not a desirable thing. There is a problem there that has to be faced. But I should like to add that, so far as I am concerned, the day cannot come too soon when the Indians will be given the federal franchise and accept it willingly.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley also said something about integration, and I must say that this is the gospel I have tried to preach in and out of season since I became minister. It was dinned into me, when I succeeded the Minister of Finance in this portfolio, by the Minister of Finance; and it is my opinion-and I think that opinion is shared by most hon. members in this house -that in the four years the present Minister of Finance was in charge of the Indian affairs branch more progress was made than at any

Indian Act
time in the history of Canada in bringing the Indians along toward integration. I have not tried to change anything very much; I have just tried to follow along the path he laid down, and this bill is simply attempting to make minor improvements or clarifications here and there along the line he started.
The hon. member for Yorkton, who said a number of things with which I agreed, did use two phrases to which I must take some exception. I do not think the Indians have degenerated, and I do not think the hon. gentleman really meant to say that. Nor do I think it is desirable that they should advance as a race; I think it is desirable that they should advance as Canadians integrated with other Canadians. I am sure that is what he really meant, but sometimes when one uses these phrases one creates in people's minds the idea of a segregation, which we do not want to have, which we are trying to get away from, but from which we cannot get away all at once, for reasons also stated by the hon. member for Yorkton.
The Indian in western Canada and in parts of Ontario-and I use the term "western Canada" in the way in which we use it in Winnipeg, not including British Columbia- are protected by treaties, and these treaties establish for them special rights that other Canadian citizens do not have. We have an obligation to respect those rights, and we must respect them in letter and in spirit.
So far as respecting them in the letter is concerned, of course, we can be compelled to do so by action in the courts; but respecting them in spirit is much more important. I do not think there is any question of the desire of everyone in this parliament to see that they are fully respected in spirit, but I hope it will also be the desire of practically everyone in this parliament to see the day come when every Indian in this country will feel that his rights as a Canadian citizen are so much more valuable than any treaty rights he has that he will not be concerned at all about the treaty rights, and when reservations, treaties and all these concepts of segregation and discrimination will have disappeared. But that is not going to happen for a long time, and it must never happen unless Indians are willing to accept it quite voluntarily. There must be no pressure or coercion. I hope that in saying this I am expressing the views of every hon. member of the house.
Now I wish to say a word about the three points made by the hon. member for Kamloops, arid in doing so I think I can deal also with the points made by other hon. members, except the hon. member for Meadow Lake in his reference to family
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
allowances. I am not quite sure that I understood correctly what he was driving at. I think there may be possibly some difficulties on this subject, so far as rion-Indians are concerned, but I know of no problem whatsoever so far as persons of Indian status are concerned with respect to the administration of the Family Allowances Act. Indian children are required to attend school wherever there is a school for them to attend, and the law is carried out in that respect. The parents of Indian children do receive family allowances for the children they are caring for. If the children are in residential schools being cared for by the government, the parents do not receive the family allowances, and one would not expect that they would.
Of the three subjects mentioned by the hon. member for Kamloops as reasons for voting against this bill, I think by all odds the most important one, iri substance, was the one relating to liquor legislation. I believe I shall wait and deal with it last, and deal with the other two first. I believe the !l t member for Kamloops had very little heart for his third point this morning. I think he was really convinced by what I said last night, and I do not intend to repeat it; but I can tell him that the suggestion he made about the making of orders in council was carried into effect by Mr. Mackenzie King in 1939. A committee of the cabinet does consider these recommendations to council, and it is in practice a very rare thing for the whole cabinet to spend much time considering any order in council; and that is as it should be. I understand that in the United Kingdom the full cabinet never considers any orders in council, and that orders in council there are passed by four ministers who meet with the Queen at the palace.
Our practice is a little different, arid we are by no means making a beginning here with the transfer of the apparent powers to the minister. I say "apparent" because the hon. member for Nanaimo is completely right in what he says, for the great majority of these orders in council that are of a routine nature. It is just a waste of many people's time to have them prepared in the form of recommendations to the council, to have them considered by several ministers and to have all this unnecessary paper work done and time consumed in producing something that is exactly what you start with.
I myself think there is a more important reason why these routine matters should not be dealt with by orders in council, and that is that orders in council should be important. The recommendations made to the governor

in council should deal with the matters to which ministers should give their full attention, but if you get a mixed bag, three-quarters or four-fifths of which is composed purely of routine matters, it makes it more difficult to find time to give proper consideration to the important matters. Hon. members will find, when we come to consider the clauses in the bill, that there is not one respect in which the minister is substituted for the governor in council that is of the importance required for consideration by a group of ministers. There is not one of them that touches anything that by any stretch of the imagination could be called rights. They merely deal with rather routine matters, or deal a second time with a matter that has to be dealt with by the governor in council or treasury board in another context.
I come to the second of the points mentioned by the hon. member for Kamloops as a reason for voting against the bill, namely that it does not provide for appeals to the courts in matters affecting Indian rights. I think the real reason it does not is that I know of no Indian right about which there is not already an appeal to the courts. There may be some; but no specific right of Indians has ever been drawn to my attention about which they have not access to the courts. However, if there are, and if there is some effective way of remedying the situation, I would be very glad to consider on another occasion-I do not think at this stage of this session in this bill-doing something to remedy it.
As far as the status of Indians is concerned, that is certainly provided for. It was provided for in the act of 1951, and we are making a clarification of that here. I know of no property rights of Indians that could possibly be affected without due legal process. This matter was not raised at all at the conference of representative Indians from all over Canada which considered the suggestions on which the bill is based. When I drew the attention of the hon. member for Kamloops to the fact that the brief from the Alberta Indian association had come long before the bill had been published he said that indicated there had not been adequate consultation.
I think perhaps I ought to say a word about that and explain what did happen. We suggested a number of changes in the Indian Act, and we divided the country into electoral districts and by a process of nomination and election had Indians chosen representative of every part of Canada. They met here in December and considered all our suggestions. I told them at the time that, of course, it would be quite improper for me to show them what would be in the bill 67509-453
Indian Act
before it was shown to parliament. I think that is a proper principle. But I told them these were the things I was thinking of recommending to parliament. There were several things we suggested that they did not like and which we dropped. There was also a sharp division of opinion about some other points. But I think I can say that, without exception, where we went ahead with any of the clauses we proceeded only where an overwhelming majority of the Indians wanted us to go ahead.
The question of appeals to the courts in some general declarative sense was never raised at all, and to the best of my recollection it has never been raised since by anyone in a general form except by the Indian association of Alberta. While of course I have the greatest respect for the self-sacrificing and devoted people who give their time to the Indian association of Alberta, I think perhaps it is fair to say that they were not quite fully informed at the time these representations were made. Of course that applies perhaps with even more force to their representations with respect to the question of liquor, to which I now come.

I stand corrected. I believe it is correct that the North American Indian brotherhood have also made the same or similar representations. I am not quite sure that they meant quite the same thing. In neither case have I ever been able to comprehend precisely how these things could be translated into statutory form. I happen to be one of those old fashioned reactionary types who believe it is better to deal with specific problems than to make broad declarations of principle which it is very hard for the courts to interpret and apply, but then I do not have the benefit of being a lawyer.
I come now to the question of liquor, and I can assure hon. members that nothing that was said this morning by any hon. member was new to me. All viewpoints expressed here this morning, and several variations of them, have been expressed to me on other occasions, from the extreme position taken by the hon. member for Nanaimo, with which I confess I personally have a good deal of sympathy, the view that the Indians should be treated exactly like everybody else and that there should be no discrimination whatsoever, to the apprehension expressed by the hon.

Indian Act
member for Meadow Lake and the hon. member for Yorkton, who seemed to feel that it was the duty of the government to protect the Indians against themselves and particularly against the provincial governments. I confess this attitude surprised me a little in the case of the hon. member for Yorkton.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: I never said any such thing. On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I referred only to the fact that instead of the federal government taking the responsibility with regard to liquor and making the practice uniform across Canada, it has seen fit in this legislation to turn the matter over to the provincial governments. My apprehension had nothing to do with the good government of the province and what that government would do, but with the fact that the federal government was reneging on its responsibility accepted under the treaty signed with the Indians. I think it would be a good idea to treat them all the same and that there should be no discrimination, but the fact remains that the Indians have not been trained-

speechtext: I am quite cool, but when Indian matters of administration are involved I may get quite warm.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
But if I did not understand him correctly then it is rather difficult for me to understand him at all. I can understand the position that we should do nothing, that we should leave the law just as it is, although that would not accomplish what the hon. member for Meadow Lake wants because he wants to go back to what the law was before the change was made in 1951. There is nothing in the proposed amendment that changes in principle what was done in 1951.
At that time a provincial initiative was established with respect to the question of giving Indians the right to drink in public places appointed for the purpose by provincial governments. We are not suggesting any new principle here at all. We are merely suggesting that

the same principle should be applied in the case of purchases of liquor in a province to be taken off the premises and consumed elsewhere in accordance with the laws of the province. I think it would be a grave invasion of provincial rights for us to attempt to legislate for Indians in this particular. Either we must have the prohibition which now exists or they must conform to the provincial law. I see no third possibility.
But we have also taken account of the fact, which I think is very well known to hon. members from all parts of Canada, that there is a feeling on many reserves on the part of the majority of the Indians that they do not want to have liquor brought on the reserves, and we are recommending a provision that in a case where the provincial law is to be applied to Indians generally, the Indians on any reserve may adopt a local option measure which would make it illegal for them to take liquor on that reserve.
It does not seem to me that this is any shifting of responsibility to anybody else except in one respect, namely that we are saying that we do not intend to give this regime to Indians generally unless the provincial authorities want it.
But in order not to deprive the Indians of the opportunity to make up their own minds in this matter, in those provinces where the provincial government does not wish to take the initiative, we are also recommending that where a band, by a vote, decide that they would like to be brought under the laws of the province instead of remaining under the Indian Act, we will consult the provincial authorities and if the provincial authorities express no objection to it-because they will have the onus of enforcing the law in such circumstances-then it will be possible to bring such a regime into existence in the particular reserve concerned.
Short of going the whole length which the hon. member for Nanaimo thinks would be desirable, though I do not think he is advocating it as an immediate measure, it does not seem to me that we could have done much better than this, except for those people who say we should have maintained the status quo. I recognize the fact that there will be strong differences of opinion in all parties in the house on this particular point. There are those who, like my friend the hon. member for Meadow Lake-and I hate to differ with him on this subject-seem to think that an Indian drunk is worse than another man drunk. I do not agree with that view at all. I think an Indian is a human being just like the rest of us. I have seen many non-Indians who were, in my opinion, just as unworthy as any Indian I have ever seen. As far as

I am concerned I do not agree with that view, but I do not challenge the right of any man to hold it. I know that my friend the hon. member for Meadow Lake holds it sincerely, and I know there are also other hon. members in the house who do so.
There are other hon. members who feel that all traces of discrimination should be done away with immediately. I believe that is the goal toward which we should aim. But I think in the meantime we must take account of the conditions of different parts of the country and of the views of different bands of Indians, and I think the latter is even more important. We know there are many of these bands of Indians who do not want a new regime, and I do not think one should be imposed upon them. Mr. Speaker, unless we want to go back beyond the act of 1951, right back to the situation which existed before that time, it does not seem to me that there is really much ground of principle on which to object to the present bill. I think I shall rest my case there for the second reading of the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall try to give this outline in completely non-technical language and as clearly as I can. I hope hon. members will grant me their indulgence if I am not letter perfect, because it is a complicated matter.
Under the present law it is competent for a provincial authority to pass an order in council to make it possible for the Indians in that province to be exempted from the provisions of the Indian Act and to he permitted to enter places where intoxicating beverages are sold legally and consume them on those premises, but nowhere else. It is now proposed to extend that.
First, the province may extend the provisions to apply to the whole or any part of the provincial liquor law. That is to say, conceivably they could make it possible- I am not familiar with the laws of all the provinces-for Indians to buy liquor in liquor stores, carry it off and consume it elsewhere in public places. If there are other ways of consuming it I am not aware of them.
Indian Act
Then if desired the provincial authorities may divide the province. That is to say, they might not want to bring in these provisions in regard to the northern part of a province because of the difficulty of enforcing the law. In other words, we are trying to make this just as flexible as possible and ease whatever problems there may be for the provincial authorities in administering the law. There is also the provision that in any province where this is done, if the Indians so desire and express that desire through the council of the band a referendum shall be held on the reserve to determine whether or not the Indians shall be allowed to bring liquor on the reserve. That is one way of approaching this problem.
We understand that there are certain provinces which have indicated that they really do not wish to be put in the position of having to take the initiative in this matter, which they consider to be a federal matter and none of their concern. They do not want to be put in the position of having to do anything about it, and we cannot force them to do anything about it. But we feel that to be fair to the Indians we ought to have a provision where the initiative could be taken by the council band.
As I recall the procedure it would work something like this. The council would indicate that they wished to be brought under the provincial laws. A referendum would be held, and if it turned out that that was the view of the band the attorney general of the province would be advised. If he offered no objection within a stated period it would then be for the governor in council or the minister-I think it is the governor in council but I am not sure without looking at the bill-to bring that regime into effect. I would anticipate that that would be almost automatic. It was felt that in a case like that there ought to be a proclamation so that everybody would know the law. I am explaining the two clauses together.

speechtext:
What the minister said at one o'clock and what he has said just now seems to make it clear that there is a situation here under which the responsibility for deciding whether or not Indians are to have liquor is clearly placed on the province. Under the proposed section 95 (1) it is made clear that Indians will be permitted to be in lawful possession of liquor within a province if that province so decides, and also that for this federal law to be effective the province has to ask the dominion government to issue a proclamation, which the dominion government will then issue. In other words, instead of this government saying we are going to permit Indians to enjoy the right of access to liquor, they are saying the province will decide whether Indians shall have this right,

if it be a right, and then if they request us to give it to the Indians of a certain province we will get it. This seems to me to be the wrong approach.
I indicated earlier on second reading that our view is that the government here should decide whether the Indians of Canada are to be allowed access to liquor, and if they so decide then they should discuss with the provinces the rules and regulations under which that will be done. This seems to me to reverse the process. The other alternative, that is the alternative of whether or not Indians will be allowed liquor on the reserves, is one in which perhaps the dominion is accepting its proper responsibility. However, this situation creates other difficulties. I would like to ask the minister how he envisages these being dealt with. It is provided that if a reserve requests a referendum to decide whether or not they should have the right to have liquor on the reserve, then providing the provincial government does not object, that referendum may be held. What I want to ask is this. There is a situation, for instance, in my own area where there are two or three reserves that would be served, if they had the referendum and it was carried and there was no provincial objection, from the one liquor store.
What happens if one reserve carries the referendum in the affirmative and the other defeats it? You have one reserve saying yes, we will have liquor, and the other saying no. Those Indians then go into a liquor store to buy liquor. How is the manager of that liquor store to know whether this is an Indian who is entitled to take liquor back to a reserve? How do the law enforcement officers deal with that situation?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
I would be glad to try to answer that question. The hon. gentleman comes from British Columbia. I think it is not unreasonable to assume, in view of the past actions of the government of British Columbia-and in any case let us assume that they would take the first alternative-the province would ask us to bring the whole liquor law of British Columbia into effect for the Indians under proposed section 95. If that were done, then the only referendum that would be taken on the reserve would be as to whether liquor could be brought on to the reserve. The Indians who lived on that reserve would be enabled to buy liquor anywhere they liked in British Columbia, and the only possible prohibition upon them would be the taking of it on to the reserve; that is in the first alternative.
Now, let us suppose there is a province like Saskatchewan which has never taken

advantage of the present law-I am just taking Saskatchewan because they have never acted under the present law-and suppose they did not act under the new law, then in that province it is a referendum of a different character which would be taken on the reserve. What the Indians would ask for on that reserve is to have the laws of the province applied to the Indians of that reserve unreservedly, and the attorney general needs to do nothing in that case if he wants the thing to go forward. There is no provincial action of any kind required. If he objected we would not hold the referendum. In other words it is within the power of the province to keep the whole province dry, so far as Indians are concerned, if they want to do so. That is the present state of affairs.
I think I said earlier that the present situation is that Nova Scotia, Ontario, Manitoba, British Columbia and the Yukon have provisions enabling Indians to drink in public places, and those provisions have been brought into force by the action of the provincial government. I would expect that in most of those jurisdictions the whole of the provincial law would be brought into operation, and the only kind of action that would then be likely to be taken under this act would be to keep a particular reserve dry insofar as bringing liquor on to the reserve is concerned. This would not mean that Indians living on those reserves could not go to a liquor store and buy liquor and consume it some other place where it was legal, just as they can go into beverage rooms and buy a glass of beer and drink it there.
I do not know whether I have made it clear, but there are two distinct kinds of referendums envisaged. One is what I might call a referendum where a province is wet to make the reserve dry, and the other is in a dry province where the purpose is to bring that reserve under provincial liquor law.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.

The result has been somewhat mixed, sir, as one would expect. I am told that the general experience in each province-I do not know about Manitoba because the experience is so very recent I have not heard anything about it-was that for the first week or so after access was given to these places a certain number of Indians abused the privilege. When the matter was
Indian Act
drawn to the attention of the law enforcement authorities, the situation was very quickly changed. Of course, there are a certain number of these people, just as there are a certain number of other people, who spend a lot of time in beverage rooms.
In that context I may say that there is no one in the Indian affairs branch from the minister up or down, whichever way you would like to put it, who wants to see Indians do any more drinking. I would far rather see them use their money for other purposes than spending it on alcoholic beverages. But we do know, and it is our experience in the administration of the Indian affairs branch, that Indians do get liquor to drink. We do know that in the places where they cannot get it legally a good many of them get it illegally, and I think there are a great many more inducements offered to them to buy illegally than any provincial government would offer them to buy liquor legally.
In addition, there is in my mind no doubt that this is another badge of discrimination and that in the minds particularly of a lot of younger Indians it is a way in which we are saying they are an inferior people. There are a lot of them who do not really want to drink at all. The hon. member for Nanaimo and I know a very distinguished clergyman, himself an Indian, who I am sure has never had a drink in his life but who is very strongly in favour of removing this badge of discrimination. I say we are not going, as I might put it, the whole hog. We are trying to effect a compromise here which will meet the varying conditions in different parts of the country.

I do think it is probably true that people who live in a rather primitive way, no matter whether they are Indians or otherwise, and who perhaps have never had a drink until they became adult, when they first encountered liquor, are rather more apt, other things being equal, to drink too much than other people who are perhaps more used to it, but of course that does not always follow.

Quite, sir. I do not think the hon. gentleman can have read the treaty very recently. I read all the treaties very carefully to see just what the provisions were and to see if this legislation would transgress them in any way. I think it is quite obvious when one reads the treaties that the purpose of the treaties was to prevent the Indians from being besotted with liquor and having their property taken away from them while in that condition, as I am afraid happened rather often in the earlier years of the contact of the Europeans with the Indians on this continent.
The hon. gentleman says that the Indians have until recently been protected from liquor. I might remind the hon. gentleman that Columbus discovered America in 1492, and I am sure he had some brandy with him. From that day to this there have always been a few people who have been willing to engage in the liquor trade and to use it in order to take advantage of their Indian neighbours.
We do not think that will be done by the provincial liquor commission in any province. We think that is done-in fact, we are sure it is done-by a certain number of illicit traders at the present time, and we feel that this proposed regime will be conducive to the integration of the Indians into our society. After all the years of protection afforded by the prohibition in the old act up to 1951, and with the limited experience we have had since 1951 with the new regime, we feel that the new regime is better than the old one.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: In reply to the minister's charge that I have not read the act very recently, I suggest that I have read it since he has.

I shall read the exact words. What I am asking is that the federal government assume its responsibility in this regard and not slough it off on the provinces. The provinces have no responsibility under the treaties, but the federal government has. The members of the federal government are the heirs, shall I say, of the representatives of the Queen who signed the treaty of 1871 in good faith. . .	. Her Majesty further agrees with her said

I am most grateful to the hon. member for asking me that most intelligent question, because I think it throws a flood of light on what really happened. I will tell the committee that when we started to discuss this matter with the Indians we intended to have a uniform regime for the whole country. However, at the conference we found that the overwhelming majority of the Indians from one province did not want the law changed at all.
I was faced with a very awkward dilemma of trying to decide whether I would go to my colleagues and recommend that we have one law for nine provinces and another law for a tenth province. I did not think that would be a very successful way of doing things. Then there was another province in which the opinion of the Indians was quite sharply divided, and it was obvious that it could not very well fit into either pattern. It was then, after a good deal of discussion with one or two of my colleagues and with a number of the officials, that we came to the conclusion that the best thing to do was to follow the pattern which had been set in 1951, and which seems to have worked very well, and allow the provinces to take the initiative.
But then I remembered that at the conference there were Indians from one or two provinces which had not taken any initiative under the law, but who themselves were very anxious to have the law changed and to have the possibility of taking advantage of the new regime. That is why we devised this second alternative of allowing a band council to make a request and of referring it to the provincial authorities. In other words, these provisions were designed in order to try to meet these varying situations. But I might say that except for the Indians of one province, or the majority of those in one province and about half of those in the other, the overwhelming majority of the rest wanted the law changed.

Mr. Chairman, maybe the minister made this matter perfectly clear to most hon. members but it is not quite clear to me. I am thinking of a case in my own riding where the Hobbema reserve is concerned, where we have three bands of Indians, to all intends and purposes, on one reserve.

Indian Act
What would happen, let us say, if the Samson and Wolf bands wanted to be wet and the Louis Bull decided they wanted to be dry? Then you would have the case of two bands on one reserve being able to take liquor into the reserve and the other band would be dry.
A few moments ago the minister mentioned the fact that so many people were willing to take advantage of the Indians by bootlegging liquor to them. In a case like this, where you would have say two bands on the one reserve who were wet, bringing liquor in, then you would have bootlegging on a scale you never imagined before, because the Indians would be bootlegging to each other. I would think that would be an extremely difficult thing to decide because, even as far as employees of the liquor store or the distributors of liquor are concerned, they would not know which was which. But the most important thing to be considered would be that those in the bands which were wet would have the opportunity of bringing the liquor into the reserve, and I am afraid there would be bootlegging on a large scale among the Indians themselves.

A few minutes ago the minister clarified one thing for me that I certainly wanted to have clarified before I voted on this measure, particularly on this section. He made it clear that by our actions here today we shall accept responsibility for giving the Indians liquor. I think that was the reply to the hon. member for Yorkton, or at least that was the gist of it.
In the first place, I am definitely going to vote against this section because I am going to have no part of putting liquor in the hands of Indians in my particular area. I have had hon. members on the other side of the house, particularly the hon. member for Nanaimo, take issue with that view. Knowing as I do his particular area and the Indians in it, particularly those Indians around the riding of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, if I happened to be the member representing that area I would take exactly the same stand they are taking. Those people already have come to the same

stage of advancement in civilization-if that is what you call it-as we have. In other words, they earn their living fairly well in the same way. If you look at the houses of the Indians around Comox, for instance, you will find that the Indians there are living in a very nice way.
To be fair with the minister I must say this, however. If I were in his position I would do exactly as he is now doing, for in that case I would be obliged to have the interest of the country as a whole at heart. But hon. members will appreciate the fact that I am not in the position of the minister, and that I represent a particular area. I am going to represent that area to the best of my ability. That being the case, I certainly will not vote for any liquor in that area. We have had the Oblate order working in that part of the country for some 160 years now to get these Indians educated and to bring improvement there. The very reason there is this difference of opinion among hon. members is the fact that there is a difference in integration of the Indians themselves with the white population in different parts of the country. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton-

should like to take just a moment to suggest that a good deal of the dubious attitude about Indians and liquor may well arise from some of the unfortunate concoctions that they were served with in earlier days. I ran into this situation when I was doing some research on the opening up of the Canadian west, particularly in connection with a place called Fort Whoop-Up, near Macleod, Alberta. It since has a different type of representative.
The fort was operated in partnership by two men on a non-partisan basis, one of whom was called Hamilton and the other
Indian Act
called Healy, who were trading with the Indians. Let me give you the recipe for the liquor which they were giving out at that time. It consisted of one quart of alcohol, one pound of rank, black chewing tobacco, one handful of red peppers, one bottle of Jamaica ginger, one quart of black molasses, and all of that was mixed well, boiled and then served to the Indians. The second alternative-they had only two types of this drink at that time-consisted of one keg of alcohol, Perry's painkiller, Hostetters bitters, red ink, castile soap, blackstrap chewing tobacco and water, all boiled together.
The reason for all the ingredients was that the Indians like firewater. They wanted something that burned, and I am sure this was very effective in that particular respect. They would trade for the mixture, one cup for a buffalo robe. I hope if the minister proceeds with this bill he will take reasonable care to see that the Indians get not only whisky, if they get it at all, but good whisky.

Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to disagree with my Saskatchewan colleagues, both in this party and in the government party, but I feel I must do so because it seems to me we are really arguing about the wrong thing when we are told that liquor affects Indians more than it does white people. I think possibly one could collect some statistical evidence to support that, but what the comparison really is between is one group of people who are economically depressed and living on a poor diet, and those who are living on an adequate diet. Really we should be turning our attention to creating conditions for the Indians whereby they will be in the position to handle liquor as well as the more intelligent members of our own race, and it is not by any means all of our own race, at that.
I do want to emphasize again the point of view expressed by the gentleman to whom the minister referred just now; but, like him, I am quite sure he has never had a drink in his life. He may have had it when he was a young man in his native village, but he is certainly a teetotaller now; but he is very firmly of the opinion that his people must no longer be protected, that they must learn to stand on their own feet and to handle this problem.
If we go on coddling them and trying to protect them we do two things. If we succeed, then we leave them open to falling by the wayside when they get out of their own primitive environment, or we encourage irresponsible and unethical people to come in and trade on their ignorance and supply them with liquor in an illegal way and under

Indian Act
such circumstances that it encourages the very sort of abuse that has been complained of here.
I think there comes a time in the life of every human individual when he reaches the age that he must be held accountable for his own actions and must be given an opportunity to develop a sense of responsibility. Our Indian people are in the same position, and I have no doubt whatever that every place where this act is going into effect one of the first effects will be a vast rise in Indian drunkenness, just as there was a vast rise in white drunkenness the moment it became easier to get liquor after the days of prohibition. But that situation has more or less corrected itself for our people, and I think we should look forward to it doing so for the Indians.
Certainly if our aim is to make of the Indians Canadian citizens rather than Indians, then this sort of restriction must be removed, and removed as quickly as possible. There is a safeguard in the bill for the Indians. When the Indians have doubts of the ability of their own people to handle this problem they can call a halt to it for the time being, and I think that should be a sufficient safeguard. I know among the Indians in my own constituency there is a divided opinion on it, and I am not sure that all of them will take advantage of this act. It is quite likely they will oppose it in some instances and in some bands, but that is an exercise of responsibility that is in line with the sort of responsibility we should expect from Canadian citizens of whatever race.
