speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this point I should like to move an amendment to provide for an additional clause dealing with the question of the right of Indians to appeal to the courts. At an earlier stage of our discussion this morning the minister said that so far as he was aware there was no case in which the rights of Indians as Indians were involved where they did not have the right of appeal to the courts as would any Canadian citizen of the white race under similar circumstances.

I do not find myself able to agree with the minister. I could well be in error here and perhaps the minister can convince me that I am; but going through the act quickly after he made that statement in order to check my previous impression it would be my conclusion that in such matters as are dealt with under the provisions of section 15, particularly section 15(l)(b) which would be a vital matter with respect to Indian rights, sections 17, 18 and 19 and the whole group of sections from 20 to 29 inclusive which lay down the terms controlling the possession of the lands on the reserves, and section 42 as well as many other sections, there is no right of appeal to the court from the decision taken by the governor in council or as it will now be in many cases the decision of the minister alone.
I would refer particularly to section 42. This is the first section of the group running from section 42 to section 46 inclusive, dealing with the descent of property. Section 42 reads as follows:
Unless otherwise provided in this act, all jurisdiction and authority in relation to matters and causes testamentary, with respect to deceased Indians, is vested exclusively in the minister, and shall be exercised subject to and in accordance with regulations of the governor in council.
Section 44 (1) provides:
The court that would have jurisdiction if the deceased were not an Indian may, with the consent of the minister, exercise, in accordance with this act, the jurisdiction and authority conferred in relation to matters and causes testamentary-
And so on.
This is the provision that the minister may transfer jurisdiction to a court, and that can only be done with the consent of the minister. There is no right there on the part of the Indian to appeal to the court from a decision of the minister in these matters. It is my view, as I say subject to correction-and if I am wrong I shall try to be fair about this and admit it-that the other sections I mentioned, for instance those from 15 to 29 inclusive, contain no right on the part of the Indian to appeal from the decision to the courts although that decision may be affecting his fundamental rights and interests as an Indian.
To the minds of those in this group that is one of the gravest discriminations against Indians and one of the greatest bars in the way of persuading the Indians that we really want them to become integrated as full Canadian citizens. I therefore move that the following section be added as section 31:
"The said act is further amended by adding the following section as section 1X2 (a) :
With respect to any decision made by the minister or the governor in council under this act dealing with any of the following classes of subjects
Indian Act
(a)	the use, appropriation or disposition of band funds,
(b)	the use, appropriation or disposition of reserve lands or of the personal property of Indians situate thereon,
(c)	the use, appropriation or disposition of any other real or personal property belonging to or appropriated to the use of Indians either as bands or as individuals,
(d)	the enfranchisement or disfranchisement of Indians or bands,
the council of the band or the individual Indian affected by the decision shall have, in addition to any other rights conferred under this or any other act, the right to appeal the decision to a judge of the appropriate county or district court or of the supreme court of the province in which the band is situate or in which the individual resides, in accordance with the rules and laws applicable to legal proceedings in that province, or, in the province of Quebec, to a judge of the appropriate superior court in accordance with the rules and laws applicable to legal proceedings in the province of Quebec."
It will be noted, sir, that the amendment is so framed that if I am in error and the minister is correct when he says there is a right on the part of Indians then the amendment does no harm, because it says that the Indians shall have in addition to any other rights conferred under this or any other act the right to appeal the decision to a judge.
If the minister intends us to take the literal interpretation of his words when he said he felt there was a right of appeal or recourse to the courts; and if there was not and we could point it out, then I would suggest that in all fairness he must accept this amendment. As I said previously, if there is a right of appeal already the amendment does not do anything. If the minister is correct the amendment does no harm. I am inclined to support the
amendment which has been moved, because for some time I have been quite disturbed at the way the sale of Indian property is handled by the department. I have made some study of some sales of Indian property in the province of British Columbia and I am convinced that the Indians were completely rooked, that the property was sold at far less than the market value. That could be done only by authority of the minister and the department.
I do not see why there should be any discrimination in right as between an Indian and his property and another person and his property. If an Indian as an individual or if the Indians as a band are of the opinion that a deal which has been made on their behalf by the department is not fair, is not in their interests, then they should have the right to appeal to the courts the same as anybody else. I shall not name the exact place, but I have in mind the sale of land from an Indian reserve on the north shore. I am completely conversant with that sale and the offers that were made and the estimates that were given by an unbiased real estate man as to the value of the property. I am certain that the Indian band lost out to the tune of thousands of dollars, yet they have no appeal.
I know there is under discussion the sale of additional property held by that same band, and if my information is correct they are not going to get a square deal in that case. As I say, that is just my impression

based on my knowledge of the facts as I have them. Whether I am right or wrong, I do say that when it comes to a matter of property rights an Indian should be in no different position from any other person. If he feels he has been discriminated against or has not had a square deal he should have the same right of appeal to the courts of this country.

Perhaps he does not realize that it is impossible for the minister or the government or any other person to sell any part of any Indian reserve unless the band has approved the sale and made a formal surrender for that purpose.
I know that in connection with the sale of certain properties in Vancouver there are certain Indians who disapprove strongly of the action taken by certain bands, contending that the bands had made improvident deals and that we should have vetoed the deals. But the fact of the matter is that no land has been sold unless the band has previously approved the sale and approved the amount for which it was being sold. Is it suggested that the minority in a band should be allowed to go into the courts to prevent the majority of the band making a sale?
Whether parliament would want to have that kind of provision in the law I do not know. It is not the law now; the law is that no part of an Indian reserve can be sold by the minister or the government or anyone else without the consent of the band properly given under the act.

Mr. Chairman, I support this amendment. On the basis of the principle about which the minister has been

talking, equality and the lack of discrimination, I submit that if we are going to bring these people in as Canadian citizens surely one of the first things we should do is to make access to justice available to all. If we are to stop these people from having an appeal to the courts of this country in order to obtain justice, we could not be acting in a more discriminatory manner. If that is not available to them, what right have we to say that we are trying to make them into Canadian citizens?
You say that an Indian can always go to the courts and get justice, but one thing that prevents him quite often from doing that is his economic condition. The vast majority of Indians in this country have not the economic means to provide themselves with representation in the courts. In many cases the funds which the band might want to use are completely under the control of the government and are now to be under the control of the minister. That is one reason we have been opposing the extension of powers to the minister to the point where he has personal touch on everything. He could quite easily veto access to the courts through not allowing them to have access to band funds.
In the interests of justice and in the interests of what is good for future Canadians, recourse to justice should be one of the first things made available to them as Canadian citizens.

I understand, Mr. Chairman, that this is the resolution on the excise tax, I want to make one of my Lilliputian sessionending speeches on this subject. I am making these few suggestions as a result of conversations with a man who has had a great

Excise Tax Act
deal of experience in the tobacco business in the United Kingdom and in Canada. I am making them to the minister because I think there is some substance in them, and I should like him to consider them when he is perusing Hansard during his summer holidays. These suggestions of mine I feel are to the advantage of the tobacco producer, and particularly to the advantage of the smokers of pipes and cigarettes-that is about the only comfort a man has nowadays. They also result in no disadvantage to the treasury and no disadvantage to the manufacturers of tobacco, if the suggestions are properly applied. What I am suggesting is the perfect idea.
I was informed that 99-3 per cent of all tobacco used in the United Kingdom is imported. This tobacco is imported in hogsheads or bales, depending on the type and source of origin of the tobacco. It is then unloaded from the carriers and straightaway placed in bonded warehouses. As the tobacco manufacturers require supplies, they simply withdraw them from the warehouse, paying for the weight of the tobacco plus the duty. At the factory in Great Britain the tobacco is processed in the normal way, but all stems, stalk, dust and so on is carefully set aside and in due course that is weighed and shipped to the British Nicotine Company at Bootle, near Liverpool, to be manufactured into insecticides such as nicotine sulphate, black leaf 40, and so on.
I think, Mr. Chairman, from the foregoing it will be readily seen that there is no reason on earth why a British firm should ever want to turn out anything but the best so far as tobacco products are concerned, because there is simply no encouragement for it to do so. The British laws regarding adulteration are also much more strict than ours, and by the very simple means outlined their products have become renowned-I am speaking of tobacco products. Because of the present Canadian excise tax laws, the tobacco manufacturer is encouraged to put as much scrap in his products as the market will bear. This also limits the amount of tobacco to be grown and causes a waste of time and labour. The public suffers by reason of poor quality and the farmer suffers by reason of the reduced production of tobacco, and the government does not gain anything.
In this country, where the excise stamp system is used, we all pay on the finished product, be it good or bad, and we may rest assured that it is no better than it has to be or the manufacturer loses his profits. In England the duty is paid on the basic leaf only and then the manufacturers compete amongst themselves, each trying to turn out a better

product than the other, because the excise system prevailing over there encourages that. Personally, I feel that even the Canadian manufacturers would welcome some change in the form of excise taxation on tobacco.
I think the change would bring the following results: it would mean an increased acreage of tobacco cultivation for the farmer, because usually there is a cutback due to overstocks of the weed. This would increase his personal income, increase his tax and better the economy of the district concerned. The second result would be a better product for the consumer by virtue of the fact that no stem or stalk would be in his tobacco, and adulteration by the addition of harsh soothers, which so often in this country are sugar, honey, molasses and so on, would be cut to a minimum or at least reduced. The tobacco manufacturer would suffer in no way. Duty-wise, the government would suffer in no way, according to my understanding. Finally, the investment in machinery would be reduced, the time of machine operators would be saved as well as the time of customs officials, printers and others engaged in the administration of the present form of collecting excise as a result of the stamps on cigarettes and tobacco.
I mention this to the minister because the gentleman of whom I am speaking had a very good knowledge of the industry in both countries and I thought there was substance in his arguments. I just mention it at this time in the hope the minister will review both the system here and the other system to see if the other system would not be of advantage to the Canadian tobacco manufacturers, the Canadian tobacco consumers, without loss to the treasury.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have some remarks to make with regard to the excise tax and the resolution in general.
In the first place, sir, it is well that we should remember how heavy a burden the sales and excise taxes constitute on the Canadian people, and any reduction in that burden as proposed in this particular clause and the second and third clauses of the present resolution will, of course, be welcome.
But, sir, there are some features of this matter that deserve further emphasis. The first is that the sales tax is primarily a tax upon goods that are consumed by the Canadian people and the bulk of the tax is levied today upon the necessities of life. A very useful study has been made recently by the Canadian Tax Foundation. It showed that of the sales tax collections of this country about 58 per cent are on consumer goods and, by comparison, only about 24 per cent on industrial purchases. Sales tax collections have been running in the neighbourhood of $650 million a year and 15 per cent of that total is levied on clothing and personal effects alone. Ten per cent of the total is levied upon household appliances, furniture and furnishings. It will be seen, therefore, how heavily this tax bears upon the necessities of life and how much it contributes to raising the cost of living to the Canadian people.
The second fact that needs to be emphasized is that a reduction in the sales tax does not necessarily mean a reduction in the total revenue from the tax. We had a very good example of this last year. A year ago the government proposed and parliament approved a reduction from 15 per cent to 10 per cent in the excise tax levied on automobiles. The result of that reduction in the rate of tax was not a reduction in the total revenue yielded to the government from the remaining tax. Actually the government derived more revenue from the remaining 10 per cent excise tax than it had collected the previous year on the 15 per cent levy.

Excise Tax Act
There is another matter that does, I think, call for some comment on the part of the minister. It is the report submitted early this year by the Carter committee, a committee of experts headed by Mr. Kenneth Carter of Toronto. That report was distributed in the house on March 26, and its importance must be recognized. The minister in his budget speech, while making passing reference to it, did not indicate what the government proposed to do in respect of the extensive recommendations contained in the report of the committee on the four broad questions that were submitted to it by the minister. These are all important subjects, and I think it is time that the minister gave the house some indication of what action the government proposes to take in the light of these recommendations.
Sir, the recommendations have much intrinsic value and their value must also be reckoned in the terms of the yield of these taxes. For the fiscal year 1955-56 the minister collected, according to his budget statement, $640 million in sales tax and $260 million in other excise taxes for a total of $900 million. He indicated that he anticipated collecting in the present fiscal year $675 million from sales tax and $265 million from other excise taxes for a total of $940 million.
The report of the Carter committee is particularly relevant in relation to the question as to the level at which the sales tax is going to be collected in the future. Hitherto it has been a tax collected at the manufacturer's or producer's level where the tax is hidden and where it has the quality of collecting one mark-up after another as the goods proceed from the hands of the manufacturer to the wholesaler, to the jobber, to the retailer and finally to the consumer. Both the sales tax and the excise tax are hidden taxes. The consumer pays them without being aware of them, and they are popular with the government for that reason. The consumer is not aware that the goods he is purchasing are subject to this tax and to the series of mark-ups on the tax as the goods proceed from the original level into the consumer's hands. Therefore what the Carter committee has had to say as to the level at which taxes of this nature may be collected is very relevant to our discussion at this moment, and certainly a statement of government policy, in the light of the recommendations of the Carter committee, is overdue.
There is one other matter on which the minister should make comment now. It arises out of the recent decision of the Supreme Court of Canada on the question of the proposed levy of sales tax on goods produced for a retailer under his own brand. The Supreme Court of Canada delivered its

judgment on June 11 on an appeal from the Exchequer Court of Canada on this point. The supreme court decided that the tariff board, before which the question had originally come, had acted beyond its powers in ruling on the question. This question was submitted by the Department of National Revenue to the tariff board and this matter proceeded on an appeal from the Tariff Board to the Exchequer Court of Canada and finally to the Supreme Court of Canada. The decision of the Supreme Court of Canada dealt with the matter of jurisdiction of the tariff board originally to entertain the question but left the question of the tax still somewhat at large, and I ask the minister for a statement as to what the government now proposes to do in the light of this decision.
I have said that we welcome the elimination of sales tax on the list of goods that are enumerated in the first three clauses of the present resolution. We are only sorry that the elimination does not proceed further. There are many examples that one could bring before this committee to establish that the minister should go much further in withdrawing the imposition of the sales tax upon commodities that should not be regarded as luxuries or indeed as anything but necessities. But I am going to deal with one subject in particular and I shall do so briefly.
The subject is by no means a new one but I think that urgency is attached to it in the light of the fact that taxes continue to be imposed upon chocolate candy, and confectionery products. The sales tax on these goods is 10 per cent. During the war, in 1942, a special excise tax of 30 per cent was applied to these goods. That tax was removed in March, 1949 but was reimposed in September, 1950, at the former rate of 30 per cent. The rate was reduced in April, 1951, to 15 per cent and, in April, 1954, to 10 percent and it continues at that rate at the present time. The industry has had to face the burden of a substantial rise in material costs, and the burden is becoming more acute because of the discriminatory effects of the tax upon Canadian producers.
In the maritime provinces there are two large plants which have not a large local market to draw upon but which are geographically favourably situated to engage in the export trade. But, Mr. Chairman, the effect of these taxes is to place those industries in an inferior position in respect of their former export trade. High tariffs in European and South American markets have restricted their exports; and in attempting to export to the United States they have been met with import duties based on Canadian home market prices which include the sales

and excise taxes aggregating, as I have indicated, 20 per cent. Recently the United states government ruled that the sales tax of 10 per cent might be deducted for customs purposes on exports into that country but that the 10 per cent excise tax must be included. This has been an important factor in preventing these Canadian industries from exporting to the United States. At the same time they have been faced with competition from overseas producers. I think it would interest the house to have one or two statistics on this subject.
Since 1942 when the excise tax was first imposed upon the candy and confectionery industry, the federal treasury has collected in excise tax from that industry over $150 million and in sales tax over $50 million. Let us look at the position created in relation to competition with importations. In 1949 the importation of candy and confectionery into Canada amounted to 5 million pounds. I just give the house round figures. In 1955 that total had increased to 25 million pounds. That is a five-fold increase in the short period of six years. It is not simply a matter of increase in population or of the Canadian people developing a sweet tooth. In 1940, when the population was 11,500,000 the per capita annual consumption of candy and confectionery in Canada was 12.17 pounds. By 1955, when our population had increased by over 4 million, the per capita consumption was 11.82 pounds of candy. Hence we can see that the Canadian producers are not holding their former share of the Canadian market.
One reason-and in my submission it is the principal reason-why they are not retaining their former share of the Canadian market is that they are being subjected to heavy and discriminatory taxes. It seems to me that this type of tax is supported, in the mind of the government, on the theory that chocolate is a luxury and not a food. To most Canadians I think that chocolate is a food and not merely a luxury.
I submit that the time has come when the government ought to take resolute measures to reduce the taxes that are being imposed today upon this product. In particular, in my submission, the excise tax ought to be removed forthwith. While the minister has not made such a proposal in his budget this year, I hope he will recognize that this matter is one of great urgency and that it requires immediate redress.

Excise Tax Act
finance charges on manufactured goods. If I recall the matter correctly, the tax is levied on finance charges where a subsidiary or an associate company does the financing. It is my view that the word "finance" in the act refers to the financing of the operation and not the financing of the sale. When a company finances the sale through ordinary finance companies and other channels beyond arm's length as it were, the money thus involved in the finance charges is not a taxable item. There is one other point that I should like to place before the minister and that has to do with the fact that sales tax is levied against work being done by the city archivist in Vancouver. There we have a very keen archivist, Major J. S. Matthews, who has made the building up of the city archives his life's work. He has run into this difficulty. Now, the provincial archives do not pay any tax at all-I presume because the federal government cannot tax provincial governments. But it does seem to me that in a case of this kind, where work is being done as a service to the community and not in any way for profit or for advertising but purely as a matter of preserving the records of the city, there should be exemption from the sales tax. The copies that are produced are given away; in fact, in some cases are given to the parliamentary library. I know that Major Matthews presented four or six volumes having to do with the history of Vancouver to the parliamentary library; and, of course, on all of the material that went into those volumes a sales tax had to be paid. I do suggest that where archives of this kind are kept by a municipality, or by any other public body, encouragement should be given by way of exempting them from the payment of this sales tax. We have all too little of this type of activity in

Excise Tax Act
Canada, and I know it would be of great help if some provision could be made in the law so that work of that nature could be exempted from the sales tax.

I think I had better be formal about this and put the explanation on the record.
This amendment to the resolution is intended to cancel the change concerning the exemption for soil pipe contained in the resolution announced in the budget speech.
The Excise Tax Act for a number of years has provided that "cast iron soil pipe and cast iron fittings therefor" shall be exempt from sales tax. Representations were made before the budget that new types of soil pipe made from substances other than cast iron are now available for use in buildings. It seemed reasonable to place these new types of soil pipe in the same tax position as the older type and accordingly the resolution as announced in the budget speech proposed that the words "cast iron" be deleted from the description of this exempt commodity.
Since the announcement in the budget speech it has come to light that the pipe made from substances other than cast iron is used for a number of purposes and there is no way to distinguish between this pipe sold for use as soil pipe and that sold for many other purposes. To restore the exemption to one which it is feasible to administer and to remove the present uncertainty in the industry it is now proposed to leave the wording of the exemption for soil pipe the way it stood before the budget speech. This amendment to the resolution will have that result.
In other words, we shall continue to have the exemption for cast iron soil pipe and cast iron fittings therefore.
On the chance that some pipe made from substances other than cast iron may have been sold as soil pipe in the interval since the budget announcement it is proposed that the bill based on this resolution will provide

an exemption for soil pipe made from substances other than cast iron sold during the period March 21 to the date of this announcement.

I am sure everyone would agree that this was a desirable amendment, sir. The law now provides an exemption from the special excise tax for articles of china, porcelain and earthenware used in the preparation or serving of food and drink. Moreover, articles for this purpose made of wood or plastic are not liable for this tax. On the other hand, articles for serving food or drink made of glass, such as glass cups, saucers, and drinking glasses, are subject to this tax if they have any cutting or metal decoration and these are in direct competition with exempt china, porcelain and plastic articles.
Since a large part of the glassware items used in the preparation or serving of food or drink have a manufacturer's price of less than 50 cents, the competitive disadvantage due to the tax was formerly not too serious but now that it is proposed to withdraw the 50 cent exemption the full effect of the tax is felt upon lower-priced glassware items. For this reason it is considered desirable to place all glassware products used in the preparation or serving of food and drink on the

Mr. Chairman, this is one paragraph which as I said is strangely incorporated in this resolution and it is one concerning which this party has registered its disapproval in the past.
I must say at the outset I have no apologies to make for the position this group has taken concerning this matter both in recent days and some years ago and it is not because of any lack of regard or concern about the development of Canadian magazines as such. We have many excellent Canadian magazines. I am not going to list any of them for fear I will leave out some small ones which are as important as some of the larger ones. I will simply comment that we have many splendid magazines in Canada that have contributed and are continuing to contribute a great deal to our general culture and progress in various ways. Their development has been somewhat of recent date as far as time is concerned.
I well recall that the party with which I was associated a few years ago, under the direction of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, did impose a general tax on all United States periodicals coming into Canada. This was a tax on those periodicals that were printed in the United States and it applied to all of them. Since that time we have seen in this country a great growth of the number of magazines sold here and there is now a circulation of some four million of the good magazines that are an inspiration to all readers in this country of which we can be justly proud.
I do not want to be misunderstood. I know there is not an hon. member in this house who is not strongly desirous of encouraging the development of Canadian magazines and seeing them flourish and assume their role of influence throughout this country.
I can well recall that in this house at the time the general tax was imposed some years ago by Mr. Bennett those who now sit to your right, Mr. Chairman, were in opposition; and I remember the hue and cry raised by the late William Lyon Mackenzie King and his cohorts, the champions of free trade and the exchange of ideas and everything else that goes to make up what he referred

Excise Tax Act
to as international good will, and their vigorous objections to having even a general tax that might apply to all the magazines including those manufactured in the United States. It must be remembered that this was a tax quite different from the one we are presently discussing.
The latter tax represents an unprecedented move. It is wrong in principle and it is bound to be dangerous in practice. It is discriminatory and unfair.
At that time Mr. King spoke in vigorous objection to the imposition of the general tax as reported at page 3880 of Hansard for 1931. It was described by Mackenzie King as:
... a tax on thought and literary art.
To the extent that the Bennett legislation was effective in blocking the entry of United States publications, it would be, Mr. King warned:
... a prohibition upon thought and ideas conveyed through these media to the people of this country.
I repeat that this was a general tax to be imposed on periodicals printed in the United States. It was not a tax on their subsidiaries in Canada. Mr. King said further, as reported on the same page of Hansard for 1931:
All advances that are made in civilization are the result of ideas, and in any way to preclude the possibility of a good idea having its opportunity of fruition to the full in any quarter is to retard to that extent the progress of civilization itself. In these days there is probably nothing more important than... that each nation should begin to appreciate the intellectual ideals and currents of thought that prevail and sway opinion in other countries. Viewed in this light the tax becomes a tax upon international good will.
He went on to say further:
I deplore any tax which will in any way restrict the widest spread of views and ideas throughout communities, particularly communities that are neighbours.
He also went on to say:
I do submit that the people themselves are much more capable of judging what they should read, what they have the right to read and what they wish to read than is my hon. friend.
He was referring to Mr. Bennett in this instance. Mr. King went on to say:
The proposed tax is one upon art, because after all art is a result of the expression of ideas. It is a tax upon invention, because invention is the offspring of ideas. To my way of thinking it is more or less a tax upon everything which makes for progress.
I am somewhat surprised, Mr. Chairman, to find that those who worship at the shrine of the late William Lyon Mackenzie King, these great champions of free trade and the free expression of ideas, the advocates of good will and all the rest of it, these people who would not do anything to provoke the

United States, who say "We must not provoke our friends in the United States", now turn around and propose to this house a resolution such as this, a part of which no one could oppose and which yet incorporates a clause that everyone should oppose, a clause that is as unfair as it is unprecedented and one that the late Mackenzie King would have deplored even more than he deplored the general tax.
If the party to your right, Mr. Chairman, could oppose a general tax on periodicals printed in the United States and being purely United States products, surely they cannot justify supporting a tax on subsidiaries of those companies here in Canada.
This tax which is proposed is dishonest because I do not think it will serve the purpose for which it was intended. I do not believe it will help any Canadian magazine. It will not help any Canadian advertisers nor will it help the millions of readers who in these days of international stress and strain feel they should know as much as they can about other countries as well as their own and obtain this knowledge in part by reading magazines printed in other countries.
The type of policy embodied in the proposal before us is totally unprecedented. There has been nothing that has passed in this house at any time that smacks as much of what one might call international provocation. This is only a sample of what happened recently in Maryland when it was proposed that a Canadian company would not be allowed to establish there because it might become a competitor to local companies and the governor of Maryland vetoed the proposition because of the danger. May I submit that as a general principle this is equally objectionable. As I say, it does not help Canadian magazines perhaps as much as they think it does or perhaps as much as the government intends it to help some of those who they think may be their temporary friends. It is a penalty, it is true, on United States subsidiaries located in Canada. Those subsidiaries share the benefits of being established in Canada, it is true, but they are corporations which pay taxes and carry obligations similar to those of any other subsidiary in Canada. It establishes a dangerous precedent by which the government can restrict competition whenever they please. With this precedent, if you see a subsidiary developing in the United States-my friends to your right practically subsidized branch companies not so long ago to come into Canada and now they penalize those who are already in here.
When it was proposed in his budget I heard the minister say what it meant to aid the development of Canadian culture; but may

I submit that there are many other articles coming into Canada in many other ways which might be considered as helping to develop the right kind of culture or encourage proper culture in Canada. I am thinking of the comic strips and the borderline pocketsized magazines which I believe in many cases have an influence upon the morality of our young readers. There has been nothing along that line.
The present government says that they want to develop Canadian culture and yet their own particular government monopoly, the C.B.C. and television, buys programs from the United States in the way of entertainment. Fifty per cent of all the programs and entertainment we have over the C.B.C. and television today in Canada are 10.0 per cent United States. Their own agency buys them and sells them to Canadian advertisers for 40 per cent less than they pay for them. Those programs are 100 per cent United States and yet they pick out two magazine subsidiary companies which are established in Canada and impose this tax upon them.
It is difficult for one to comprehend why this is done. Not only that, they say that the gross advertising revenue of these magazines will be taxed 20 per cent if there is any advertising in the magazines which does not appear in the non-Canadian magazine in the United States. There was a general tax in effect and when Mr. King came into power that government repealed the tax altogether because it had been condemned so vigorously by them. On March 13, 1936 when the Bennett tax was revoked by this government Mr. King had this to say to Mr. Bennett:
I would ask my hon. friend whether as a matter of fact the tax was not just one more protectionist device intended to limit competition rather than promote the development of culture?
Mr. Bennett replied as follows:
I assure him that protection was not the question; it was a question of having foreign advertising in Canada make some contribution to the country. I want to be fair.
You can see the distinctive difference between the two types of tax. The government of that day was saying, as vigorously as the Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King could say, that they opposed this general tax on publications which were printed 100 per cent in the United States; yet now we have a government of the same party trying to re-establish a tax on a special few, you might say on two magazines, because 25 per cent of it is the same as if printed in the United States.
Surely if we are going to try to encourage Canadian culture the C.B.C. and television should not buy 100 per cent United States

programs and sell them at a loss of 40 per cent to the Canadian taxpayer. What this government now proposes to do is to subsidize 100 per cent programs by their own agency and penalize two subsidiaries of United States companies because they are carrying 25 per cent of a certain type of advertising. I hold no brief for any magazine in Canada, as these magazines do not need any brief by me.
We have excellent magazines such as Saturday Night, Maclean's and many others. They have developed and will develop. These magazines represent more than four-fifths of the total magazine reading in Canada. There will be about one million people who will wonder why this penalty is imposed upon Time and Reader's Digest. We have many magazines in this country which have developed, as every hon. member knows. I have read Reader's Digest and Time and they are newsy magazines. They contribute a great deal with their ideas as to what is going on in that country and as to what is happening throughout the world in these days when international good will and international knowledge are more important than at any time in our history.
It seems to me that if a quarter of a century ago it was wrong to place a general tax on magazines which were not being taxed in any other way, surely if that was considered a curtailment of the freedom of the press to a degree, if that curtailed the dissemination of knowledge and ideas of international good will you might say to the extent emphasized by the late Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, how much more would it be so today in the case of these subsidiaries established in Canada and having all the rights of any other subsidiary. They are being singled out and told that they must pay a 20 per cent tax if 25 per cent of their reading matter is similar to what is printed in the United States. Even if it is not, even if it is all Canadian reading matter, if they advertise something in Canada which they do not advertise there-the minister shakes his head, but the last section of the resolution reads:

It is indeed passing strange, Mr. Chairman, that this government, which has warned so long and so loud that we must not provoke the United States, and that is the reason they cling to that dusty old doctrine of free trade in everything, in the exchange of goods and ideas, should now propose such a clumsy and discriminatory

Despite the fact that the textile producers, the rubber footwear people and many other branches of industry have been pleading with this government to do something for them, and in spite of the fact that this government pose as the champions of freer trade-almost world champions at GATT and every place else-in spite of the fact they pose as the champions of free trade, the freer exchange of goods and ideas, they now propose a clause such as this. I urge the minister to reconsider this clause. I urge him to delete this clause from what is otherwise a sound, progressive step in repealing taxes which 1 think should have been repealed long ago.
Again I say that in this unprecedented move we have you repenting, in one case, for having imposed the sales tax that you said you never would impose, then you turn around and impose a tax that you formerly condemned, a tax on magazines. I believe that United States magazines coming in here should pay something, along with our own magazines. Again I say that to impose a tax such as this is unsound, unfair to subsidiaries and dangerous in relation to good will. It is extremely provocative. You are trying in vain to help a few and most disastrously affecting only a couple of all the United States periodicals. There are several other reasons I could advance to the minister, but if he will take no cognizance of the ones I have given I shall not delay the house by telling him any of the other reasons why this clumsy protection should not be adopted by these champions of free trade.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry indeed that the minister has no statement to make because there are a number of matters of importance to be discussed in connection with immigration and there are a number of criticisms to which his department has been subjected with respect to its immigration policy over the past year and we would have liked to hear the minister's views on them. I think it would have made for a more useful discussion. However, there is no way in which we can compel the minister to make any statement so I will have to present the criticisms and make the suggestions that we have in mind.
A few days ago I asked the minister for figures as to the number of immigrants reaching Canada in the first six months of this year. kOn July 24 an answer was given which ;shewed that in the first six months of the -years 1954, 1955 and 1956 respectively the number of immigrants arriving in Canada was 85,765, 58,417 and 69,938, with the total for June of 1956 being estimated, but I understand that will be very close to the actual total. We are pleased to see that there has been a small improvement in the figure for the total of immigrants landing in Canada for the first six months of 1956 as against the first six months of 1955 when the figures were disappointing in the extreme. But I do not think there is room for very great satisfaction in that the figures are still appreciably below those for 1954 and the figures for 1954 were in turn quite appreciably below the figures for 1953.
Therefore, although we have what might be called an arresting of the downward trend from 1953 to 1955 inclusive we have not gone very far yet towards recovering the high point of immigration which was in the years 1952 and 1953. I am under the impression that one of the reasons for the improvement that is to be noted is one or two ways in which immigration policy has been changed and greater inducements or assistance held out for immigrants to come to Canada. These have not gone anything like as far as we would like to see them go as yet but I think they should be remarked on and I feel bound to observe that it is in some respects again a policy of too little and too late.

One of the matters which we in the official opposition had been pressing for a number of years was an extension of the assisted passage loan scheme with respect to immigrants from the United Kingdom particularly but also European countries to cover the members of the family instead of its being confined, as it used to be, to the head of the family only. We pointed out and pressed as strongly as we could that there were numbers of cases where in our view lack of assistance to the members of the family resulted in potential immigrants declining to come to Canada because, although the head of the family could come out, it meant that for an appreciable time, perhaps a year, perhaps as much as two years, his family would be separated from him and that when immigrants were weighing the pros and cons of a decision to emigrate to Canada that factor might and almost certainly would be a very powerful determining factor in arriving at their decision.
Constantly and consistently the department through the minister-when I say "department" I wish to emphasize that I mean the minister because he assumes the responsibility-took the view that this was not a well founded argument. In fact, I recall being told that it was considered that it would perhaps be more to the advantage of immigrants under these circumstances for the breadwinner to come out ahead and get himself established in Canada and then later, when he was in a position to do so, send for the other members of his family. It was strange that not more than a few months after the last time that statement was made to us officially in the estimates committee when considering the minister's department last year the department suffered a change of heart and the policy was reversed. The very thing which we had been told it was neither desirable nor practical to do was in fact done and the provisions of the assisted passage loan scheme were extended so that dependent members of families of proposed immigrants could be assisted under the scheme. I think it is a coincidence which we are bound to discuss and to which we are bound to direct attention that not long after that change was made there was observable some improvement in the figures with respect to the number of immigrants coming to Canada.
I do not want to be petty about these things. I would say that any change is better late than never. I mean that. I am glad that the department has changed its policy in that particular. I think we are entitled to say-in fact, I believe we are bound to do so- that this result demonstrates the truth of the assertion that we have often made,

namely that the minister is not really taking all the steps that could and should be taken to encourage and to facilitate immigration into Canada. The unfortunate part of this matter is that, during the years when they refused to take this simple and sensible step, there were lost to Canada large numbers of desirable immigrants who found it easier for them to go to other countries, such as Australia in particular, which extended to them facilities similar to those now being extended at this late date under our assisted loan passage scheme.
If one analyses the figures with respect to immigration into Canada and into Australia, one will see that they demonstrate beyond doubt that Canada has been lagging behind and has been suffering because of the lack of an aggressive policy in encouraging immigrants from the United Kingdom and, to a considerable degree, immigrants from other countries in Europe.
I also recall that we used to be told that we did not want to do what Australia was doing in respect of encouraging immigrants, that they were finding that their policy of extending generous assistance to the immigrants in meeting their passage was not working out, and that Australia was receiving a large number of undesirable immigrants. The inaccuracy of this assertion or this defence of department policy is proved in the light of the fact that Australia has just recently re-embarked upon a further five-year immigration program. I am quite sure the minister would not wish to accuse of irresponsibility the government of Australia or that of any other country. It therefore cannot be maintained that the Australians have found that among the immigrants they were getting were a large number of undesirables, because to say so would be to assert that the Australian government was irresponsible in the extreme in repeating that experiment or in fact in increasing their efforts in another five-year program to get immigrants from the United Kingdom on an assisted basis. Canada has therefore been suffering as a result of a weak government policy with respect to the encouragement of immigration into Canada.
I noticed a report in the Montreal Gazette of January 13, 1956. It shows that it is not only by the United Kingdom that preference is being shown for Australia but it is being shown by other European countries as well. This is a dispatch from Geneva. It is headed "Many Immigrants" and reads as follows:
Geneva-Australia has replaced the United States as the principal area for resettlement of Europeans migrating to new homes under international auspices. During 1955 nearly 54,000 persons were resettled in Australia by the intergovernmental
House of Commons
committee for European migration. This was 45 per cent of the total number of people aided by the committee during last year. The United States was second on the list of reception countries with 20,523 migrants assisted by the committee. The committee is a 26-nation agency which offers shipping, screening and other services to countries interested in promoting either emigration or immigration.
Some tentative criticisms have been advanced against us here because it is said that we have been saying that we should copy Australia and that Australia gets the bulk of her immigrants from the United Kingdom. We have not been saying that we should copy Australia in every detail, but we have been saying that we compare badly with Australia in terms of aggressiveness of our immigration program. It is now demonstrated that Australia's immigration program is not confined to immigrants from the United Kingdom. As we see, nearly 54,000 persons were resettled in Australia from Europe in the year 1955.
Surely it cannot be said that the opportunities in Canada are inferior to those in Australia for the settlement and establishment of immigrants. If such a thing were said, I would certainly deny it. That being the case, where is the blame to be laid for the fact that we do not get as many immigrants to Canada as Australia gets? I think the answer is inescapable. I think the blame lies at the door of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and that the responsibility rest? with the minister who declines to inaugurate-and follow through sufficiently aggressive policies to bring immigrants to Canada.

The company has been operating in Canada for some years under the name Personal Finance Company. I think that as a parliament we should be careful in allowing companies to use names that suggest that the company itself, by some means or other, is going to hand a favour to its customers or provide something that is beneficial or in the customer's interest. The name should be a neutral name, I suggest, and it should not be something that will convey the wrong impression. I do not think

The new rates, good as they will be, are still high. They range to as high as 2 per cent per month on loans up to $300, or 26 per cent per year, and even in the area of the smallest loans, on loans up to $1,500, the rate will be 1-27 per cent per month, or something in excess of 16 per cent per year, so that the rates that will be *charged are still high and will still be a very substantial burden on the customers. People in this country know quite well what kind of business is being undertaken by small loan companies, and the kind of business they are operating. The rates they charge have been given a great deal of publicity in parliament and in the country this year, and the small loan companies are smarting from the publicity they have been given, so that there is a move now by this company to change its name from "Personal" to "Beneficial".
The small loan companies even wanted the name of the Small Loans Act changed to consumers instalment credit act, something else they thought would give them a better name in the eyes of Canadians generally. If we are to be consistent as a parliament in attempting to curtail not only the excessive rates-but some of the practices of these companies in promoting larger and larger numbers of loans at higher rates of interest, I suggest we should refuse to allow this company to change its name.

The house in committee on Bill No. 166, to incorporate Signature Loan and Finance Company-Mr. Richardson-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Incorporation.

subtopic: SIGNATURE LOAN AND FINANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill is to incorporate a new small loan company. Although it is my sincere belief that there are already too many facilities of this sort for the extension of small credit, I am not going into the arguments concerning why I feel this way but it is an inflationary matter. I understand that our instalment credit has now exceeded $2 billion. I am not in favour

of the encouragement of this particular type of credit. I propose at the moment to suggest a better way for people who do need a service of this type to obtain it.
There have been a great many revelations both in the committee and in the experience of many hon. members as to the effect that the use of some of these small loan facilities has had upon family life and the economy of working people. I suggest the reason they use this type of accommodation in many cases is that they do not know other types exist which would be more beneficial, and when I use that word I mean it would be more beneficial in relation to themselves and their families.
I admit there are people who have to seek accommodation in order to pay their doctor bills and, in provinces not so fortunate as my own, in order to pay hospital bills and that type of expense. They think they have to have money by which they can consolidate their debts although how they lessen them by consolidation I really do not know. So far as I am concerned, consolidation is only a method of increasing one's debts to a considerable degree.
I think it is true that something in excess of 50 per cent of the people who use this type of accommodation for the consolidation of debts return after the consolidation has taken place because they need more money with which to consolidate their new debt.
My suggestion is this. The price people pay for accommodation of this sort by way of interest is too high and I think this has been stated clearly enough. It has always been a mystery to me what 2 per cent a month means but I obtained an explanation from an authority in the committee. I understand it is 26-8 per annum. I observed that the brief of the Caisse Populaire puts it at a slightly lower figure, 26-46 per cent per annum; but I think those two figures are close enough that we need not quarrel about them.
We in this group feel that the banks of this country are not performing a sufficient service in the field of small loans. The Bank of Commerce does cater to people requiring small loan accommodation and the bank has a system of discounting which I do not like. It increases the interest rate but the result is that people can borrow money for between 10 and 11 per cent per annum and that is certainly less than half what they would have to pay for similar accommodation, a loan of $300 or less, if they obtained it from a small loan company.
When the manager of the Canadian Bank of Commerce appeared before the banking and commerce committee as a witness he said there was a profit in this particular

business at that rate of interest. We think the banks of this country could very well fall into line with the policy of the Canadian Bank of Commerce and engage in the extension of small loans if only as a social service. They have admitted that while they are performing a social service they also make a profit. When the president of the bankers' association was asked why other banks did not participate in that particular field he said it was because they gave a different interpretation to the act to that given by the Bank of Commerce. I may be wrong, but I believe the Bank of Commerce has been carrying on operations of this sort since 1936 and I would imagine that if the legality of their operations was going to be questioned it would have been questioned before now. I think probably the answer is that the other banks have lots of business without taking on this type of thing. While it is profitable it is perhaps not as profitable as some of their other business and they are not too ready to indulge in it.
Since I am opposing the incorporation of still another company to provide these small loans I would point out that this is the type of service which can be rendered by the credit unions of this country and their counterparts the caisses populaires. The credit union is perhaps particularly favourable to this group in that it does translate the cooperative principle into small loan financing. The differences in the philosophy, shall we say, of the two sets of people, the credit union and the small loan company, is considerable. The first aim of the credit union is not to lend money but rather to promote and encourage thrift.

I point out again in connection with this clause that this is going to be yet another company owned by people outside of this country. It will operate in this country and will borrow money from Canadian banks presumably at the present rate which I believe is 41 per cent. It will then lend money to those unfortunate people who find it necessary to borrow and who are ignorant of the existence of other institutions which would be healthier for them. They will be charged interest at the rate of 26-8 per cent. To me that is a rather serious matter. These people just do not know; these people just cannot do the mathematics. We were told quite candidly in the committee by the president of the small loans association of Canada that he was quite convinced that under the stress of circumstances these people would borrow even if the interest were double or even if it were half the present rate. They just would not pay any attention to that particular part of the transaction.

subtopic: SIGNATURE LOAN AND FINANCE COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I oppose this clause and I oppose this bill because I believe we already have too many companies in the small loan field.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SIGNATURE LOAN AND FINANCE COMPANY
speechtext: Competition.

subtopic: SIGNATURE LOAN AND FINANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance says "competition" but the competition in this field is placing a greater burden upon the borrowers in this country. We have already too much "competition." Every morning over the radio we hear the advertisements of these small loan companies. "Come in and take out a loan." "Come in and talk to Harry, he is a fine fellow with a good personality, it will take but half a minute and you can walk out with whatever money you may need." That is the kind of competition and advertising you get from the people in this field who are burdening the borrowers in this country with extortionate rates of interest. This so-called competition is not competition in fact, it is just competition in name and it does not benefit Canadians at all. I think that the Bank of Canada statistical summary clearly shows that we have already too many companies in this field exerting too much high pressure salesmanship. Parliament, rather than adding to the number of companies in the small loan field

by granting a charter to another company, should be adopting further means of controlling this field and of reducing the interest rates that ordinary Canadians generally have to pay.
I oppose this clause for another reason, and that is the name of the company, the Signature Loan and Finance Company. I can already hear what they will do with that name in their advertising. Nothing to getting a loan; just a matter of your signature. Come in and sign; no security, no chattel mortgages; just walk in and we will take you over as long as you give us your signature. I think parliament will make a mistake if this bill should pass. I do not think we need to provide additional facilities of this kind. There are probably already too many companies in the field. Certainly, the growing number of companies in the field and the growing number of branch offices is causing the superintendent of insurance some concern. He pointed out in the committee that there are more and more companies interested in doing business in this field. Far from being discouraged by any move to reduce interest rates, apparently more companies have been encouraged to go into this field. He pointed out that from December 31, 1954 to December 31, 1955, the number of branches of small loan companies in this country increased from 540 to 702, an increase of 162 branches. We do not need any more competition, as the minister has said. You already have a very great number of branches; you already have too much pressure from small loan companies in this field, and I believe we would be wise to turn down this bill.

speechtext:
At five o'clock I had just dealt with the facts which established that Canada is not getting as many immigrants as she should have or as she could get because the Department of Immigration is not pursuing a sufficiently aggressive and realistic immigration policy. The figures I have placed on the record are amongst other evidences that go to substantiate this statement. In our view this is one of the very serious deficiencies in the policy of this government in that connection. They are not exerting sufficient efforts to bring to Canada a sufficient number of desirable immigrants, neither as many as we could get, as many as the growing economy of Canada requires nor as many as it could absorb. We believe it could absorb a considerably larger number and that until we bring our population figures up to the required level we will constantly experience difficulty in supporting standards of living that our people demand and which the resources of the country make it possible for us to realize. A country's greatest asset is, without question, its people. Canada has benefited in the past from those who have come here from other countries. I would hope that statement itself would not be challenged and I will therefore not enlarge it further or seek to support it by argument, but leave it there and say that it is regrettable we are not getting more people.
In case there should be any tendency to question our realism in saying that immigration, particularly under the present circumstances, could be of immense benefit to the country, I should like to place before the committee a letter which I should have noticed before because it was written in 1955, but it just came to my attention the other day. It was written by the father of an immigrant to Canada from Scotland who had, apparently previous to that, written to the Hamilton newspaper asking for comments
67509-455J
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration from people living in Canada as to whether or not it was advisable for his son to emigrate to this country. Apparently the majority of the answers were in the affirmative. Plans were made and the boy set sail for Canada. By the time this letter was written he had arrived in this country. The letter was written to the Hamilton Spectator and it was published in full oh Friday, May 20, 1955 as follows:
To the Editor:
Will you permit me through the courtesy of your columns to thank the very many people who so kindly wrote to me following your publication of my letter asking whether my son ought to emigrate to Canada?
Most of these letters were heartening. Most of your readers said: "Yes, by all means let your boy come out." So we have done.
A week ago my wife and I stood in driving rain on the seafront at Gourock and watched the Franconia glide down the Firth of Clyde. We waved until the ship was out of sight. That ship was full of emigrants like our own son-all dreaming of the new country they were sailing to and all, I suppose, a little fearful of the unknown that lay ahead beyond the western wave.
We have given our boy enough money to keep him afloat for a few weeks until he gets himself a job. We have told him to take any job, even street sweeping, until he gets a foothold and can look around him.
He has never been away from us before. My wife and I, in fact, do not quite understand why our son wants to emigrate at all. For there are plenty of jobs in Britain at good money-columns of vacancies in the newspapers here every day. Britain is crying out for workers but the strange-lure of Canada seems to exercise a spell overyoung minds that will not be denied.
Then I am skipping some portions of the letter. It continues as follows:
One word more. When we send our children out to Canada to fend for themselves in the pioneering, spirit that made Britain and Canada great, all we ask is that they be given a fair deal and a chance to prove themselves.
We seek no charity and no favours for them and certainly no preference. But we think that our young British boys and girls have something to contribute to the fabric of the Canadian nation that cannot be purchased with gold.
Here, speaking if I may for myself, I would interpolate that so do the other immigrants who come to Canada contribute something, from whatever country they come, that cannot be purchased with gold.
The Scots brought you caution and business acumen. The Welsh and Irish gave you the saving grace of poetic imagination that is the very soul of a people. The English, with their genius for compromise, gave you the gift of good government.
Sir, that can be enlarged to include the arts and crafts that have been brought here and the many skills, too numerous to mention, that have been brought to Canada by immigrants from countries in that old land of Europe. These are the ideas which I think should be in our minds as we welcome these

Every ^emigrant ship that touches your shores carries on board a potential prime minister. So it behooves Canada to welcome her young immigrants, however poor they may be, for they are rich in many things that a growing country needs and needs badly.
Sir, it is interesting to think of that for a moment or two. I was about to point out that there are in government at the present time others who are immigrants to Canada, and in that respect I think we should be rather proud that we place no obstacle in the way of people achieving the highest position in Canada. I am not going to criticize what the Americans like to do and they will make their own regulations for themselves, but I think it is a rather remarkable contrast that in that country one requires to be born in the United States, a citizen of the United States at any rate, in order to reach the position of president. Here in Canada we impose no such barriers and I would hope never would impose such barriers.
But as these immigrants have so much to offer and have offered so much, the main architect of confederation himself an immigrant into Canada, I think we should occasionally take stock and reflect whether we are doing enough to attract these immigrants into Canada and to set them on their feet when they arrive here. That leads me again to a criticism of the policies of the department both with respect to its attitude towards getting large numbers to come here and with respect to some of the details of administration, because immigration can be discouraged not only by a policy which does not seek to attract them in large numbers but ean also be discouraged by the attitude taken to those who land here as reflected in their treatment by the department and departmental officials. If there is a bad record of treatment of immigrants to Canada, then that is going to discourage others from following their example.


There are, unfortunately, a number of cases in recent years which have indicated clearly that the administrative practices of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration with respect to its handling of prospective immigrants are-well, they have been described in the newspapers on previous occasions as shocking and unfortunately there are too many of these practices referred to last year which still persist to lead us to believe that the adjective should be changed. These are not cases merely of maladministration in isolated cases in the sense that they turn up from time to time without anyone having brought the practices which give rise to these cases to the attention of the department.
We have brought to the attention of the department on numerous occasions the very situation which is bound to create this type of case in the policy pursued by that department. I refer, of course, particularly to the refusal of the department to inform prospective immigrants who are rejected of the reasons for their rejection, which practice is carried over in a number of cases to a refusal to inform people who land in Canada and against whom orders for deportation are made of the reasons for those orders. We have said before and we say again that this practice is absolutely unjustified, that it is contrary to the principles of justice upon which this country's system rests.

speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would permit a question at this point.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when a minister is guiding his estimates through the house I know he expects to hear the views of hon. members and also perhaps to hear some criticism of his department, or of the policy that his department is carrying out. I hope I will not disappoint him in that regard. However, before I speak on some

of the policies that I think should be mentioned I should like to express my appreciation of the minister and of the fact that he gives his personal attention, or he has given his personal attention, to the many cases that I have had to bring to his notice.
Since I represent a constituency in Vancouver, British Columbia, I seem to receive a great many immigration problems. I refer them all to the minister. He always pays attention to them, and although he sometimes takes many months before a decision is reached, at least every two or three months he writes to me and explains he has not forgotten them and tells me why there is a delay. I want to say I really am thankful for that consideration. I am also exceedingly grateful that upon occasion he reverses the decision of his department. I have had success in cases that I have brought to his attention, but not in all of them. It is on a number of these cases that I should like to speak this evening on this item.
I want to deal, Mr. Chairman, with the question of East Indian immigration and also of Chinese immigration and with some of the problems that apply to them. I believe that all British Columbia members are in a good position to speak on the East Indian question because 95 per cent of all of the East Indians in Canada are in the province of British Columbia, and the majority of them are on the coast. I think it should be noted that of the majority of the East Indians in British Columbia by far the greatest number of them come from the Punjab.
Punjab, as you know, has been referred to as the fighting state, and those people have been referred to as warriors. Throughout their history they have proven their right to be known as warriors. They have proven it on behalf of the democracies in a great many wars; they have proven it over many years on behalf of the British commonwealth. They are British subjects and here in Canada they are Canadian citizens. I completely fail to understand the thinking of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration when a person who is a British subject and a Canadian citizen is discriminated against when it comes to the question of immigration. In view of the desire of the government for immigration into this country, in view of the fact that we can support a far greater population than we have at the present time, and in view of the regulations with regard to East Indians, we can come to the only conclusion that there must be a colour prejudice somewhere. We find that, strangely, enough, in dealing with the land of origin of East Indians, it is a matter of treaty as to how many can enter Canada as of right; but in addition to that,
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration regulations are made under the authority of a statute of this country, as regards East Indians, which provide that in a year the number of immigrants from India permitted to enter Canada is 150, from Pakistan 100, and from Ceylon 50. These regulations are very definite. East Indians do not have the same rights as the Latin-Americans and as the Levantines when it comes to the age at which they can bring in children or their mothers or their fathers.
Something is definitely wrong when British subjects, as the East Indians are, are placed in a depressed category along with those other categories that I have named. Not only are East Indians British subjects, not only do we have them in Canada as Canadian citizens, but, sir, they are good British subjects and good Canadian citizens, and I am certain that every member here from British Columbia will tell you that. Then, why should they have so many obstacles thrown in their way in getting their relatives into this country?
I have in mind, just as an example, one of the finest citizens of British Columbia, an East Indian, yes. He was one of the originals in Canada. He came to British Columbia some 48 years ago. He has built up an excellent business. Unfortunately, he has no children. He is getting on in years and he wants to pass on his property to a Canadian citizen. He wants to bring in his nephew and to adopt him as his son, establish him as a Canadian citizen and let him carry on in his business. And yet, although the application has been under process for years, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration refuses point-blank to allow this one citizen of British Columbia, who is childless, to bring in his nephew. I think something is definitely wrong in the attitude of the department in matters such as this.
I am not going to go into all the details of the brief that was submitted by the East Indians to the minister some two weeks ago because he knows the content matter of that submission; but I should like to quote from the last two paragraphs on page 3 of the brief because I feel their request is just and should be given speedy attention. It says:
If being a British subject and having commonwealth ties is to mean anything, then it should mean that all within the commonwealth should be placed on a uniform basis, so that Indian citizens should be accorded the same privileges, say, as Australians and New Zealanders.
Alternatively, we submit that as Canadian citizens the very least that we should ask for is that we should be treated no worse than Latin Americans and Levantines, and that we should be given the same rights that they are given as to bringing in relatives. We ask that regulation 21 be widened to let in relatives of Canadian citizens of East
