Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Indian origin, to the same extent as regulation 20	(c) admits , Latin-American and Levantine
relatives.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, our East Indian Canadian citizens in British Columbia are not asking too much when they ask that the government, or the department, give them a status as British subjects no less than that which this government and this department are giving, under the same authority and regulations, to the Latin-Americans and Levantines. Since it does not require any amending act of this House of Commons, I sincerely hope that we can this evening or before these estimates are through, have a statement from the minister that he very speedily will bring in the required changes in the regulations so as to give to our East Indian colleagues in this country the rights they have been so long denied.
I wish to say a few words at this time, Mr. Chairman, concerning the matter of Chinese immigration. I received a great many immigration cases from Vancouver and I take these problems up with the minister. He has been good enough to say that I have a very high batting average on the cases I take up and I am exceedingly grateful for that.
It is most difficult to understand the thinking and the policies in some respects as far as the department is concerned on matters that relate to Chinese immigration problems. I would like to give just two or three examples to show what I mean.
I know of the case of a young man of Chinese origin who was born in the city of New Westminster. He spent his life and received his education in New Westminster. He served all through the last war with great distinction. When the war was over he took advantage of the rehabilitation measures and set himself up in business. He built a good business and succeeded in it and then proceeded to build himself a home and furnish it. At this point he is ready to take a wife.
This young man's fiancee lives in Hong Kong; but do you think he could get permission for his fiancee to come to Vancouver in order that this young man could marry her? The answer is no. We offered to post any bond that would be required to ensure that when she arrived here she would marry this young man. The answer was no. In a letter I wrote to the minister I personally gave my word of honour that if the minister would permit her to come to Canada we would be prepared to post any bond he might require, and I went so far as to say that we would keep the girl confined in the immigration shed until she was married to this 

young man and that if she did not get married to him she would be returned on the next plane to Hong Kong. What was the answer?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
The answer was no. This young man is a wonderful citizen; he has established himself in business and has built and furnished a home. Instead of paying $550 for the passage of his fiancee from Hong Kong to Vancouver he has to secure someone to look after his business and then pay $550 for the flight of his fiancee from Hong Kong to Vancouver and in addition to that he has to pay $1,200 for his own passage to Hong Kong where he will marry the girl and return with her as his wife to Canada. Why should this be necessary, sir? Surely a matter of this nature could be attended to on a different basis.
Another example concerns a Chinese gentleman who has been in Canada for many years. It is customary to go back home to China and take a wife and beget children. This man is all alone in Canada in his old age. He has only one child in Hong Kong and he is supporting the boy and trying to bring him over but owing to the technicality of the son's age the answer to his request was no.
We who knew this Chinese citizen-I knew him>-were aware that he was dying and one reason he was dying was because of sorrow, and therefore we got in touch with the minister. A number of us, people who dealt at his store and knew him well, got together and agreed to put up the money for a bond if this young man in Hong Kong could just come to Canada and see his father who was dying in hospital here. What was the answer?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: The answer was no. I might inform the minister that three months after I wrote to him concerning this case the old man died in hospital in Vancouver.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: Will the minister go to heaven? No.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
In view of the fact that we citizens who are white-if that should make so much difference-were prepared to put up the bond to guarantee that the young man would return to Hong Kong after a brief visit with his father, why should the department be so sticky that they could not allow an old man with no family in Canada an opportunity to see his only child?
Now I would like to speak on the major phase of the subject of the Chinese immigration problem. Why this almost complete insistence that immigrants should come in as

a family unit? I refer to it as being almost complete because in recent months the minister on two or three occasions has reversed previous decisions and has allowed families to come in not as a unit. But, as I understand it, the basic policy of the department is that the family come in as a unit.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman would not mind my correcting that statement.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: I think the rule is that we do not admit children unless both the parents are here or unless the parent who is in China comes with the children.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: But we do not insist on the whole family coming in together.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: You insist on their coming in as a unit, though; the parent and the child or the parents and the child.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: Of course they do not come at all unless one parent is here.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
That is exactly what I am coming to. If you could only learn to control that impatience a little bit!
The only way you can emigrate from China is from Hong Kong to Canada. Because of the governmental situation there the relatives of many of our Canadian citizens of Chinese origin are in communist-held territory. From all the information I have been able to obtain, it is exceedingly difficult for them to get into Hong Kong where they can go through the necessary examination by the officials of the department and receive the required authority to be admitted to Canada.
I have heard that in the past Canadian citizens of Chinese origin were actually being blackmailed; that is, they had to pay somebody in the village in order to get their wife or children into Hong Kong. Sir, I am convinced from my contact with Chinese in British Columbia that this is true and the practice still prevails. Because of this and the difficulty of getting into Hong Kong you cannot always get all the children, or the children together with the mother, out of the country at the same time. Sometimes it is spread over a period of years and very frequently over a period of months. In some instances you can get a child into Hong Kong more easily than an adult.
We have situations such as this. I will refer to a specific case because then the minister will understand to what I am referring. I am speaking of an agreement with the minister's department that the wife and children of a certain citizen in Vancouver
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration can come to Canada. However, the wife and one child have not yet been able to get out of the village in which they are living into Hong Kong. One five-year old child was able to get out of the village and has been in Hong Kong now for several months living with a relative. Just why, when the child is separated from its mother and father, can the father in Vancouver not be permitted to receive his child who has been living in Hong Kong for almost a year?
The minister has just recently given me a decision to the effect that the child cannot be admitted until the mother can get to Hong Kong and both she and the child can go for the examination before the authorities in that city. Concerning matters of this nature I just cannot understand where is the milk of human kindness in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and some of its officials. I often wonder whether they have been fathers themselves, and I sometimes doubt that they have. Otherwise they would not put obstacles in the way of these people as they seem to do.
I know that there are regulations, I know that there must be a close check, and I know that those who are coming in from China must be watched closely because of the conditions there. I believe the minister and the government know-I have had some indication of this-that in the past couple of years there have been people coming in who perhaps should not have been permitted to come in. If my information is correct, some of these people are using Canada as a causeway into the United States. Be that as it may, I am certain the department is keeping a close watch on all cases such as I have mentioned.
But where the department is agreeable to people coming in, why do they insist that they cannot come in except under the condition of all or none? They must come in at one time instead of being permitted to come in as they can get to Hong Kong and be processed by the department. I do not want to repeat myself too much because that is a bad habit of mine, but I should like to plead with the minister just to think over some of these things and see if he cannot give greater consideration to this matter of the immigration of relatives of our Chinese Canadian citizens. I am quite certain it could be done without in any way endangering this Dominion of Canada and it certainly would make a few individuals very happy to have at least part of their family with them if they cannot have them all.
There is only one other point I wish to mention, the matter of cash bonds. In this connection I am still waiting for a conclusive

Excise Tax Act
reply from the minister. I am not a member of the legal fraternity but I understand that the courts will accept bonds other than cash bonds. However, the immigration department insists on cash bonds. I am told by lawyers in Vancouver that if you happen to arrive at the airport after five o'clock the officials will not accept a deposit of cash because they say there are no facilities for handling cash bonds between five in the afternoon and nine in the morning. Although the immigration department is prepared to let you in under bond you must stay in the immigration detention cells because there is nobody authorized to take your money. To me that is a stupid state of affairs. I hope sincerely the minister will do something to correct it and also give some consideration to having the immigration department accept the type of bond acceptable to the various courts of law in this country.
I see that my time is almost up and I will stop at that. But I ask the minister to show a little more of the milk of human kindness in handling some of these cases and to realize that perhaps there is too much red tape in his department. If he could get rid of that I am sure the department would be much more popular than it is at the present time. Finally, I repeat what I commenced with. Let us not have discrimination between British subjects and Canadian citizens because of the colour of their skins. Let us give to the East Indians their just rights. I ask the minister to use his power at the next meeting of the governor in council so that the regulation may be amended to permit our East Indian colleagues in British Columbia to bring their relatives into Canada.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I propose to say a few words about the bill, but assuming as I do that there is not very much disagreement if any with respect to the clauses other than the one having to do with the magazine tax I shall confine myself to some brief comments on that and at a later time when I conclude the debate make references to

what has been said this afternoon by the Acting Leader of the Opposition.
I should like to point out to the house that in proposing a magazine tax we are not proposing any tax or tariff on the ordinary editions of magazines as published in their home countries. Those magazines will continue to flow freely into the hands and homes of Canadians. However, we are concerned with the so-called special editions of magazines which are much the same in their reading content as the editions of the same magazines published abroad but which, in a way that seems to us unfair, are making inroads into the revenues available from magazine advertising in Canada.
I should like to remind the house that the position of Canadian magazines has been brought to the attention of the government and parliament on many occasions over a considerable number of years. Particularly during the past four years the growing difficulties of Canadian magazines have been urged upon us. We have attempted to give them some positive help. The various government departments were asked to give special attention to Canadian magazines in placing their advertising whenever that medium was appropriate. We considered assistance in the form of special concessions on postal rates, but decided that once again the amount involved would not prove significant. We have continued to watch developments closely. We have seen two things which have given us real cause for concern, one related to circulation and the other to finance. First, a word or two about circulation. We have in Canada only a dozen or so magazines of general interest which are widely read, including those published in the French language as well as in English. I am speaking of course of the sort of magazine one finds on any well-stocked newsstand; I am not speaking of the numerous magazines catering to specialized trades, professions and other groups in the community.
Since the war a few of these general interest magazines have gained circulation, one or two quite spectacularly; others have made little progress; one or two have disappeared entirely; and two have cut down their frequency of issue. In the aggregate their circulation has increased, but this increase cannot compare with the increased circulation in Canada of general interest magazines originating abroad. Thus the proportion of Canadian to non-Canadian magazines read in Canada has been falling steadily. This is the main point of concern.
Shortly after the war about one-third of the magazines of general interest read in

Canada were Canadian; four years ago the proportion was down to one-quarter; last year it had fallen to one-fifth. I wonder if there is any country in the world where only one-fifth of the magazines of general interest are of national origin and four-fifths originate abroad.
The second point which has impressed itself upon us is financial. We have received figures over the years indicating quite clearly that the publication in Canada of these magazines of general interest is not profitable. The figures we have received were of course obtained in confidence but I can assure the house that they were disturbing. I can disclose that for the year 1955, when business in general in Canada was good, and when our leading Canadian national magazines had larger aggregate circulation and larger advertising revenues than ever before, those published in English made not a profit at all but a loss estimated at 2.4 per cent of their total revenue. Those published in French are too few to quote percentages but the house can be assured that their position was about the same as that of the English magazines.
It must be clearly understood that this tax is designed to assist not the publishing house necessarily nor the printer but the magazine itself. In many industries, firms add or drop different lines of production, depending on their profitability, without causing any concern to themselves or to their customers. Their balance sheets are better off for the change, and their customers find other sources of supply to meet their needs. Canadian magazine publishers would similarly be better off financially to drop a number of their general-interest magazines and concentrate on the profitable lines of their business; and, without some assistance to make these magazines profitable, that is what they can be expected to do. Failure to grant this assistance would not mean that these publishing houses will go out of business, although some of the smaller ones might, but it would certainly result in the eventual disappearance of a substantial proportion of the few remaining Canadian magazines of general interest.
Before trying to find remedies for the ills, we tried to diagnose them; and it soon emerged that they faced two quite different forms of competition from abroad. One may be described as overflow circulation; the other is the special edition.
Excise Tax Act
I believe-and I agree with what the Acting Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon-that, given a fair chance, the Canadian magazines should be able to stand up against the overflow into Canada of magazines published abroad for circulation in their home markets. True, those magazines are usually prepared for far larger markets, at far greater expense; they pay far more for their articles and their stories; and they can spend more money on their pictures. Nevertheless, attractive and interesting though they may be, they are not Canadian; they are addressed to a somewhat different audience; they advertise a somewhat different range of goods. So the Canadian magazine, with its distinctively Canadian material, should be able to hold its own against them in the Canadian market. It may tell its story less expensively, but Canadians want to read it and will continue to want to do so as long as it can afford to put out a vigorous and attractive product.
This is where the other type of competition, the competition of the special edition, is so damaging, for these editions can and do cut at the financial foundations of the Canadian magazines-their revenues from advertising. Some people, both inside and outside this house, have expressed doubts on this point, and so perhaps I should quote some relevant figures.
There are, as I have said, about a dozen magazines of general interest published in Canada, including two special editions. These dozen would, I believe, usually be taken to include the following: Canadian Home Journal, Canadian Homes and Gardens, Chatelaine, Maclean's, Mayfair, La Revue Moderne, La Revue Populaire, Le Samedi, Liberty, Reader's Digest (special editions in French and English), Saturday Night, and Time (special edition). How have the two special editions fared within this group? We find that eight years ago these two special editions attracted about 18 per cent of the advertising revenues of the group; last year they attracted 37 per cent. Mr. Speaker, I should like to have consent to put on record a table showing the figures in detail.

The two special editions that I have mentioned are not the only ones in the field. Of recent years several women's magazines, of the type usually distributed through chain stores abroad, have decided to put out special editions on sale in Canadian stores. The names of these special editions now on sale here are: Family Circle, Woman's Day, and Everywoman's. Similarly, Parent's Magazine puts out a special edition for Canada. These editions sell advertising space to cover the Canadian market. If these sales of advertising were included in the figures of magazines of general circulation, the proportion of Canadian general-interest magazine advertising now going into special editions would be about 40 per cent.
However, that is not all. Before deciding to impose the new tax, we had learned that at least two other well-known magazines published abroad were making plans to put out Canadian editions in order to attract Canadian advertising. Further, in connection with one of these projects, a well-known publisher of trade papers abroad was known to be considering the establishment of a branch in Canada; thus the field of trade papers too, which has so far been relatively profitable and in which there have been only one or two small special editions, would be open to serious invasion by special editions.

We have had a number of requests for exemptions, and, as the bill will indicate, there are a number of exemptions, but I need not deal with them at the moment. The question was whether or not the government ought to give consideration to imposing a tax not, as has been indicated, on editions of magazines coming from abroad, which after all, as I have pointed out, may possibly not compete unduly, for the reasons I have given, but whether or not the real difficulty facing the Canadian publishing industry might not be confined to the special editions. After giving it careful consideration, we decided that such a tax would be in order. Perhaps the result will be that there will be an equalizing effect in the competitive situation, although, of course, I cannot say how much it might affect individually each of the special editions which have been published in the past or which might be published in the future.
I should emphasize that the proposed tax will apply whether the special edition is printed in Canada or abroad. As I stressed in my budget speech, the publication and circulation of Canadian magazines is a thread in the fabric of our national life. If we wish to see Canadian magazines continue, we must find some technique for arresting the inroads into advertising revenue made by these

special editions. A special edition printed in Canada constitutes as much of a threat to the existence of Canadian magazines as does a special edition printed abroad. It is for that reason that we propose that the tax should apply to special editions wherever they may be physically produced.
There have been some suggestions that this is a discriminatory tax. Indeed, the Acting Leader of the Opposition mentioned that this afternoon. I propose to leave it at that by saying that it is not discriminatory and I shall confine myself to answering his statement later in that respect. However, I want to place before the committee one fact, namely, that it is extremely doubtful that there is any country in the world so situated in this particular regard as Canada. We are next door to a tremendous market and a tremendous outpouring of magazines of all kinds, whether for reading material or for advertising. I think the house will agree that under these conditions it is only to be expected that our own publication industry would have difficulty, but this is particularly true when our languages are alike, our tastes are alike and our pursuits, whether by way of recreation or occupation, are much the same.
Therefore I should like to say that this tax cannot in any sense of the word be called an anti-American tax. The purpose, of course, is to apply the tax to all forms of special editions, whether they originate in the United States or not. The motives behind the tax, I think, have been made clear, but I think it is overlooked that, if anyone supposes that this tax would in any sense of the word offend our neighbours to the south, it would seem to me that the obvious answer would be that if the North American continent is to be strong-as we all ought to hope it would be- that should mean that Canada and the opinions of Canada could and should be independent and that, if we are to have a public opinion in Canada other than that which we would gain from our newspapers and our own discussion, it can only be fostered and continued by a periodical industry which would have critical opinion on many subjects, both internal and external. If we foster that, then our own independent opinion will be the more valuable; but if that opinion disappears we have nothing then to offer except a repetition of the ideas of someone else, and I do not think that the house would like that under any circumstances.

There are, of course, in the present bill many other provisions than that pertaining to the proposed tax on advertising revenue of certain magazines with special editions. With those
Excise Tax Act
provisions of this bill other than those pertaining to the tax under discussion we have, of course, no quarrel. On the contrary, at the resolution stage of the measure this afternoon we expressed our gratification at seeing in the bill exemptions from the sales tax introduced in favour of many commodities. However, I shall follow the example of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) tonight and confine my remarks on second reading to the proposed tax on advertising matter. I wish to recall to the house what we have said in regard to the bill in general by way of putting this discussion in its proper perspective.
The views of Her Majesty's loyal opposition with respect to this tax were stated in the house on April 10 by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) when he spoke in the budget debate. His remarks on this subject are to be found at pages 2782 to 2784 of Hansard. Other hon. members of this party also expressed their views in the course of the budget debate, and the views of this party were reasserted this afternoon at the resolution stage by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) as Acting Leader of the Opposition. Sir, those views are firmly held.
What is the essence of this provision in the bill? We may well see it in its context if we recall the introductory remarks of the Minister of Finance in the budget debate in leading up to this subject. On March 20, as found at page 2333 of Hansard, the minister said, after describing the magazines coming into this country:
We have been considering this problem for some time, and we have decided that, in this field, very exceptional measures can be justified-measures that certainly could not be justified in connection with any ordinary line of business or commerce.
I ask the house to note well these words. The minister has decided that the measure of which he now asks approval by the house is one which could not be justified in connection with any ordinary line of business or commerce. The measure itself he describes as very exceptional. That, Mr. Speaker, is the estimate placed upon this proposed tax by the minister who has fathered it. It is indeed a measure which could not be justified as applied to any ordinary line of business or commerce. This proposed tax is indeed a special tax on a special group singled out of a particular line of business, and therefore I say this is a special form of governmental interference with the magazine business.
The house will not have forgotten that the resolution was first introduced in the house on March 20. We are debating it now on August 7, about five months later. What has become

Excise Tax Act
of this resolution in this long interval? Why was it not pressed forward at an earlier date? We had other resolutions arising out of the budget speech of the Minister of Finance before us on earlier occasions. Why has this one been held back for so long until we are virtually on the eve of prorogation? I suggest that the reason is that the minister found he had something of a tiger by the tail and he did not know what to do with it. He has been embarrassed by it and that is the reason he has held it back until this moment. He has been asked repeatedly in the house to say whether or not he intended to proceed with the tax. On every occasion his answers have been coy and evasive. However, there is one thing that the house has learned to expect and that is that neither the minister nor any other minister of the government is prepared to lose face, and so rather than submit to anything like losing face the minister has decided to press this measure in the dying moments of the session in the face of a virtually unanimous public outcry against the proposed tax.
I should like to analyse the proposed tax and to state to the house certain facts that stand out in any fair and searching analysis of it. In the first place, this is not a tax for revenue purposes. Normally taxation is designed to serve the purpose of raising money, but it is not pretended by the minister that the raising of money is any part of the purpose that he has in mind in fathering this new tax. No, this tax is to serve some unusual or abnormal purpose. Something other than the ordinary purpose of taxation is what he has in mind. What is it? I shall seek to answer that question a little later.
The second fact that is outstanding on any analysis of the bill is that it is not a general tax. It is a tax of particular effect. The statement has been attributed to the minister that there might be nine magazines or thereabouts affected by this measure, but certainly it is undeniable that the two that will be the hardest hit are Time magazine and Reader's Digest, the latter in both English and French editions. I understand that the gross advertising content of these two magazines in the form of Canadian advertising produces a revenue of about $6 million per annum. This is not a general tax. It is a tax of particular application.
It is patent on the face of it, therefore, that this tax is discriminatory and, sir, I do not know that there is any worse vice to be found in any form of tax than to find that it is discriminatory. The party of hon. members opposite was critical 25 years ago of the tax applied by the Bennett government on United States magazines entering Canada but, sir,

that tax of the Bennett government was a uniform tax applied right across the board. It was not like this tax, a discriminatory imposition.
The third fact that is outstanding on any fair and searching analysis of this tax is that it is a new kind of tax. In our taxation of corporations we are accustomed to thinking in terms of a tax on income which in the case of corporations means a tax on their profits. But this is not a tax upon the profits of the corporations which publish these particular magazines. This is a tax on advertising revenue; in other words, it is a tax on a particular form or source of revenue of these taxpayers. That fact adds to the discrimination that is inherent in this measure.
If you want a parallel situation here is one. It would be if the Minister of Finance decided to apply a tax on newspapers in this country and he did not choose to apply it on profits but chose to apply it on advertising revenue to the papers. There is a parallel. Does any hon. member in this house support such a parallel? I do not believe there is an hon. member of the house who for one minute would be prepared to lend his support to such a proposal and yet that, sir, is the type of tax that we are asked to approve here and now.
The fourth fact that stands out with regard to this measure is that the minister has chosen to apply a rate of taxation of 25 per cent-

It has no relation to any fact or situation that the minister has placed before the house.
I come now to answer the question that I asked a little earlier. What is the purpose of this tax? It is not to raise revenue. A review of what the minister has said tonight and what he said on March 20 indicates that the minister's purpose is to help Canadian periodicals, as he says. But how? Not directly, of course. His purpose, as embodied in this tax is, as he asks the house to suppose,

to help Canadian periodicals by hurting United States publications which print Canadian editions here in Canada. That is the purpose; and in relation to that purpose we have nothing in the way of a yardstick by which to estimate or judge the propriety of a 20 per cent imposition.
The next fact I observe is this. The house has been given no proof that the growth in the circulation of United States magazines in Canada which would be affected by this tax has hurt Canadian magazines. The minister has assumed that fact; he has not proved it. Just because there are United States magazines which are printing Canadian editions and because, as the minister asks the house to believe, the rate of growth in the circulation of Canadian magazines has not kept pace with the total market, although it has grown absolutely, he asks the house to assume that the latter fact is attributable to the former. Mr. Speaker, the house will require in the way of proof something better than the minister has offered. He has just asked the house to swallow an assumption for which he has offered no proof.
The fact is that Canadian periodicals are increasing their circulation and their advertising revenues. The industry is becoming stronger. When my leader spoke on this subject on April 10, he put on Hansard, as reported at page 2784, some of the figures on the size of the circulation of Canadian publications in comparison with the two United States publications with Canadian editions which are going to be principally affected by this tax. May I remind the house of what he said:

Growing twice as last as fast-growing Canada. Audience now 1,836,000. Circulation up 66 per cent since 1946. Population up 31 per cent.
These Canadian magazines are not asking for the sympathy and the dreary expressions of lack of confidence in their future that we have heard from the Minister of Finance here tonight. We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition are glad indeed to think that the Canadian periodical publications are showing such vigour and vitality. We have confidence in their future.
The next fact that I put before the house is that we have been given by the Minister of Finance no proof whatever that this tax will indeed help the Canadian magazines. There is no proof that the imposition of this tax on these particular magazines will stop advertising in them. Indeed, having regard to the fact that many Canadian businesses operate on a fixed budget for advertising, it may well be that when this tax is passed on to the Canadian advertiser by the magazines on which it is imposed in the first instance the net result will be that the Canadian advertisers will not reduce their advertising in those particular publications, but will, if they continue to operate on the same advertising budgets, reduce instead the advertising space that they are purchasing in the Canadian publications; and the end result of this tax may well be not to help Canadian magazines by hurting the United States publications, but actually to hurt the Canadian magazines. Do not take my word for it, Mr. Speaker. Here is what has been said by the general manager of the Association of Canadian Advertisers in an open letter that he wrote to the Minister of Finance on April 3, 1956. I do not think any hon. member of this house can maintain that he is in as good a position to judge of the effect of this tax upon the advertising business and the advertising habits of Canadian advertisers as is Mr. Frank A. Again I say, Mr. Speaker, it is perfectly apparent that this tax abounds at every turn in discriminatory features.
Sir, what has been the reaction in this country to the proposal made by the minister with respect to this tax? The reaction in this country, as may be judged by editorial columns right across the country, has been strongly hostile to the tax. Indeed, the strength of that hostility, both in the quality of expression and in the widespread sources right across the country in which it has been expressed, is almost unparallelled, with the possible exception of the reaction editorially to the government's program a year ago on the defence production measure and on this year's pipe line measure, with all that happened in the course of the debate. The publication I had in mind was Modern Medicine of Canada, a very highly respected medical publication which has been published in Canada since 1946 and which has a British edition with Canadians on the editorial board. This publication because of having a British edition would have been affected by this tax and I could not believe, Mr. Speaker, that the minister would propose to apply a tax such as this on a magazine of this type. I therefore said, as reported at page 2650 of Hansard for March 27:
We do not like discriminatory taxes. There have been protests already from the United States sources and there have been many Canadian protests. As was inevitable, there are some magazines which evidently were not within the thought of the minister when he proposed this tax and which are now pointing out that they are going to be affected by it. They are not among those which were referred to in the press or in the talk that went on around the corridors. Of such are magazines whose chief purpose is such as the dissemination of medical information, magazines edited by competent medical sources.
The Minister of Finance cut into my remarks at that point to say:

I think it points again to the dangers inherent in such a tax. There may be many more worthy magazines which will turn up that may be affected; not commercial magazines at all but professional

Excise Tax Act
magazines or other worthy non-commercial types of magazines which none of us may have in mind at the moment.
We are faced with the necessity of making a decision on a new tax, an unprecedented tax, a roundly renounced tax. This is not a tax that is being applied at the outset of a new undertaking in Canada. This is not a case of saying to persons who might be contemplating the opening up of Canadian editions of their magazines in Canada, "We are taking note of the fact that you are introducing something new, are engaging in a new enterprise; if you do that we are going to tax you." No, this is a case of applying a new and discriminatory tax to an enterprise that has been in operation and is established. The effects of discrimination under circumstances like that are all the more reprehensible.
I say, sir, that the minister has not been fair in this matter. By his coy and evasive answers in the house, by the elusive tactics he has practised with reference to this resolution ever since it was introduced nearly five months ago, the minister has left those who are going to be affected by this tax wondering whether or not he intended to proceed with the tax. We think they should not be made to suffer for the indecision or the procrastination -whichever it may be; perhaps both-of the minister.
Having regard to the fact that advertising contracts, as the minister must know, are written months in advance, I think that if he is determined to proceed with the tax and if the majority of this house should regrettably support him in this intent he ought to give consideration to deferring the operation of it for some further period to give an adequate opportunity to those who are going to be affected to make their forward contracts.
The bill is going to give wide powers to the Minister of National Revenue to make regulations with respect to the tax. We do not like that kind of legislation.
Let me say this, sir, in conclusion. We as a party do not yield to any party or anybody in this country in our concern for the fostering in Canada of a truly Canadian culture. It is quite true, as the minister has said, that the relationship between Canada and the United States in this particular is probably unique in all the world, with a great country alongside a smaller country speaking the same language.

The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that I was completely aware of the medical journal he refers to and I had given careful consideration to it before the budget address was delivered. I can assure the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) that when I interrupted him I did not do so for the purpose of pulling the wool over his eyes because he finds it difficult to see some things in any event.
Secondly, both the hon. member for Eglinton and the Acting Leader of the Opposition seem to have some kind of faint cry of help for the Canadian publishing industry though they wanted it to be their particular kind of medicine that the industry would have. There was a nostalgic appeal to the Bennett regime and the way they had taken action to impose a tax on all magazines coming into Canada. If there ever was a tax that could be described as a tax on ideas it would have been that one and not the present tax.
This party when it attained office in 1935 repealed that tax and I am glad to know that

while I listened pretty intently I did not discern very much evidence in either speech which would indicate that they thought we were putting a tax on ideas at this particular time. It is true that in some of the editorial comment immediately after the budget address that idea was given a good deal of credence, that this was a tax on ideas, and the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) used that considerably in her address, but that idea is dissipated with the knowledge of what the tax is intended to do in connection with the magazines on which it is to apply. No one has suggested that we are impeding the flow of ideas; indeed I do not think that assertion can now be made in the light of what is intended by the legislation.
This afternoon the Acting Leader of the Opposition used the word discriminatory, and so did the hon. member for Eglinton tonight. He made the point that the Bennett legislation applied to all magazines coming into Canada, and that that was not discrimination, whereas this is because it applies not to those coming in from abroad but to what we call the special edition magazines. I pointed out to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) that when he referred to what Mr. King had done in 1935 or thereabouts he was referring to editions that did not exist at that time. The present so-called special editions did not start in Canada until 1942 or 1943 and this was not a problem with which Mr. King had to contend, nor even Mr. Bennett for that matter. We have it on our hands now because it has developed in that time and it has developed in a way which I do not think anyone in either 1931 or 1935 could have foreseen. I think the purpose of the tax is perfectly clear and if I did not make it clear to the hon. member for Eglinton, I shall do so now.
The tax is made necessary because of the fact-this fact is not disputed by anyone, not even the Canadian association of advertisers, about which more in a moment-that the peculiar nature of the special editions makes the editorial cost of producing material infinitely lower than that of the Canadian publication. That is the purpose of the tax, and perhaps the only purpose because in some manner, as I said in the course of my remarks earlier tonight, there will be equalization from this tax.
Reference has been made to the letter written to me by the Canadian association of advertisers. I interjected during the course of the reading of that letter to point out that the association expressly disavowed any intention or desire or perhaps ability to solve the problem with which we

were contending. They said that they had no comment to make on how to deal with this particular matter. When they called on me they reiterated what they had said in the letter. I appreciate hon. members' desire to curtail the debate and I intend to follow that desire. Since this is going to be a straight affirmative or negative vote, I should like to put one or two other points before the minister that may still persuade him to change his mind. I should also like to take issue with one or two statements he made earlier in the debate. In the first instance, the minister suggested that this was not really a tax on advertising. I do not think it can be called anything else and I suggest to him that is one of the principal reasons why the business community of Canada has taken such strong exception to the tax.
Paragraph 9 refers to a tax of 20 per cent of the value of advertising material contained therein. It is a tax on advertising, and the greatest lubricant, the greatest single force responsible for taking the goods produced by our modern economy and making them available to more and more people has been advertising and merchandising. I think most of us will agree with that. Therefore anything which tends to increase the cost of advertising and make it more expensive tends to decrease its utility and usefulness and to impede our industrial progress and our progress as individuals towards higher standards of living. I am not going to labour the point because I see the minister nodding his head which I hope means he agrees with me, but basically because this tax is looked upon as a tax on advertising it is viewed with considerable distress, opposition and antagonism by the majority of business in Canada, and

I think that has been reflected in the editorials that have appeared in the papers and in the representations which have been made to the minister.
Having said that, I should like to refer to the fact that the minister made certain statements regarding the very poor position in recent years of certain Canadian publications. He has an advantage over us in that respect because practically all these organizations are closely owned and do not publish their financial statements, as the minister knows. Therefore he has information which is not generally available. I would point out to him. however, that in at least one or two cases such as Saturday Night Press, which does publish a financial statement, their publishing business is only a portion of their overall operation, and while there has been no indication that that particular company is doing well there has been no indication either that the blame may be laid at the door of their publishing business. It could very well be because of their printing business.
But turning to the minister's specific worries about the growing difficulties which these companies have been experiencing over the last four years, some of these companies have published observations on their progress and we find statements like this in Canadian Advertising for March, 1956:
Maclean's . . . are today harvesting sweet fruits . . . advertising investment in Maclean's is up 117 per cent since 1950.
In the same edition of Canadian Advertising the Wallace Publishing Company states:
Jet propulsion . . . when in the brief span of a decade a company grows to 25 times its original size.
Weekend magazine states in the March 23, 1956 issue of Marketing:
Weekend magazine in 1955 topped all other magazines in advertising dollar volume.
Floyd Chalmers, president of Maclean-Hunter Publishing Company, states in the Financial Post of May 23, 1955:
For the 13th successive year Maclean-Hunter has shown an increase in gross business over the previous year .	.	. gross revenue was $16-2
million.
Mark this:
Since the beginning of 1955 two publications have been started .	.	. we now publish four
national magazines.
The Financial Post of March 26, 1956 reports the following:
Canadian magazines have sold $17-4 million worth of advertising space in 1955-$1-3 million over the previous year.

Finally, Marketing for January 13, 1956 reports:
There's a good year ahead for magazines . . . some of the more optimistic publishers see dollar boosts of from 20 per cent to 50 per cent . . . Magazines roll out the red carpet.
I suggest to the minister that in the light of such remarks those people who have persuaded him that Canadian publications generally have been experiencing growing difficulties during the past four years may have overemphasized their particular situation to him. It is very easy. The minister has heard these representations, but to the best of my knowledge and that of the trade he heard them almost primarily from the one side and not from the other.
The minister suggested that the government had done their best to channel advertising revenue into Canadian magazines in order to help them. It was only last Friday that we noted and passed in the house an expenditure of $980,000 for travel advertising in magazines by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and every cent of that was specifically dedicated to United States magazines. A portion of ihat money could well have been spent in Canada to persuade Canadians to travel in their own country rather than go south of the border. If that is an example of the help which the government has been giving to Canadian magazines, I do not think it is very realistic and I must doubt that the minister's colleagues have actually been supporting him in this idea he has put forward.
The minister indicated his concern over the growing circulation in Canada of general magazines from outside Canada. Unfortunately I have not got any statistics at hand on the growth of circulation of magazines from outside our borders, but I would suggest to the minister that the growth of Canadian publications has not been too poor.
Twenty years ago Canadian periodicals sold 1,059,000 copies a month. Ten years ago they sold 10,899,000 copies a month, and last year Canadian periodicals sold 18,173,000 copies a month. These are very sizeable increases. They represent a growth of more than four times in 20 years, a growth which has far outstripped our Canadian population.
It rather indicates that despite whatever circulation increase may have been achieved by United States magazines, our Canadian magazines have also been doing well in that field.
The minister also indicated that the tax was designed to assist not the publishing house but the magazine. The only way in which I can deal with that argument is to say that it sounds to me like doubletalk
Excise Tax Act
because every magazine is owned by a publishing house and is controlled by it; and any assistance which goes to a magazine goes equally to a publishing house.
Fourth, in dealing with the minister's statement I would point out that he speaks about his worries with regard to the total disappearance of the few remaining magazines of general interest here in Canada. In that connection-and again to show the minister that the Canadian publishing industry has been doing quite well on its own feet-I would point out to him that in 1935 there were 57 Canadian consumer magazines of one sort and another.

Excise Tax Act
that those figures show the minister that the magazines are not disappearing from the Canadian market but rather that they are coming more and more into the Canadian market and that the publishing industry in Canada is well able to look after itself.
Just today, Mr. Chairman, figures came to me indicating that, despite this difficult position which the minister puts forward for the Canadian publishing industry, they are able to compete and are actually able to raise their advertising rates. If you are able to raise your rates, that is an indication that you are in a strongly competitive position. In the first six months of this year, of our Canadian consumer magazines there were 9 which increased their rates and one which decreased them. Of our business publications there were 30 which increased their rates and none which decreased them. Those figures would seem to indicate strongly, Mr. Chairman, that our Canadian magazines are successfully meeting this competition and that in most cases at this point they do not need this type of protection which is so invidious and so unsatisfactory, as was pointed out by my colleagues.
I am not going to labour the point further, Mr. Chairman, but there is one thing I hope I shall not hear from a government which has at one stroke with this tax done grievous harm to two fine publications, namely Reader's Digest and Time magazine plus a number of others which are less well known. I hope that same government is not going to come out and, under the guise of talking about what they have done for Canadian culture, leave the Canadian public with the impression that their attack has been directed against Modern Detective Stories, True Love Stories, Esquire, The Police Gazette, Modern Scientific Stories and many others-I could give the minister a list of 100 publications of that sort-which are flowing across the border into Canada every day and which are contributing nothing to our culture, to our advancement or to our civilization. Instead of taking any broad approach to this matter, the minister has singled out the two publications I have mentioned in the full knowledge that one of them has been one of our best Canadian industries and businesses, spending over $6 million a year in this country and employing over 600 Canadians. To my way of thinking, Mr. Chairman, it is something of which this government can be little proud.

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to express my own personal views on this matter very briefly. A while ago, on the resolution stage, I asked the minister what criterion or method would be used to define the words "the same or substantially the same" as they

refer to the editorial material in the so-called special editions. His answer was far from satisfactory. In addition to that, I feel that this is definitely a protectionist move disguised as something different. It is an attempt to tax the advertising of the special editions in order to fulfil the avowed purpose set out by the minister himself, namely to assist Canadian magazines which, he said, were losing money. We have no figures to show that they are losing money but we must take his word for that.
What I do not like in that respect is the special statement "to assist Canadian magazines". There are many desirable Canadian magazines that I should like this government or any other government to assist. But when you say "to assist Canadian magazines" and stop there, what does that mean? Does that mean that every Canadian magazine printed and published in Canada is a desirable magazine, so much so that it is more desirable than is anything printed in these special editions? The minister does not think so and I do not think so. Yet, without any way of separating them, this is a move to assist all Canadian magazines, some of which may be absolute trash. There are some that are trash and we know it. Why should we make a blanket provision to assist any kind of literature published in Canada just because it happens to be published in Canada? As a matter of fact, I have seen some Canadian publications which contain nothing more Canadian than many of the United States editions that come to this country. That is one ground on which I feel that this is a clumsy and deceptive provision.
In the second place, what would be the effect of taxing this advertising? It may not be of any assistance whatever-in the long run-to the Canadian public because, if this protection goes through, and if the Canadian magazines wish to take advantage of the fact that there is that protection on this type of advertising, the result may be that they will just raise their advertising rates and take up the slack or take up the difference, and then the competitive position will disappear. Personally I do not think that this tax will have any effect on the number of special editions sold in Canada. All it will mean is that there will be a higher cost to the consumer of that material in Canada. Then, on another ground, and to me this is rather important, it is left to the Minister of National Revenue to define or to decide what is meant by the term, "the same or substantially the same". With all due respect to the Minister of National Revenue, either the present one or any other minister, I do not think that he is competent to decide what is meant by the words, "the

same or substantially the same", when it comes to editorial material.
Then, there is exemption for material which is principally for religious or medical purposes. Well, the hon. member for Eglinton has already pointed out that here you have wide-open possibility for discrimination. Why not educational material? For that matter, why not scientific? There are many people who might think that scientific material is far more important than medical material. Why not agricultural material, and so on? There is almost an endless list that you could add to that. I think it is' leaving much too much discrimination in the hands of the Minister of National Revenue, and it is a clumsy and half-baked way in which to try to do something which might be desirable but which, in my opinion, this one certainly does not accomplish.

That is the essence of our objection; not that the department does occasionally have to exercise some judgment as to whether or not people are admissible-it has to do that *-but our objection is that the department exercises the judgment without giving the subject of the inquiry a proper right to state his or her case. Had that right been given in this instance this misunderstanding and the ghastly consequences from the point of view of the woman's reputation and peace of mind would never have taken place. Mr. Chairman, it is not my
intention to take very long tonight in making my observations but I would like to say the reason why I am not going to take so very long is not the reason given in an article in the newspapers today which stated that the Social Crediters are always complaining about the business of the house going so slowly.
I do not think we have been doing too much complaining. We have been participating in the debates and have been doing our best to present the views of our constituents. Certainly, however, we do not feel that we have to prolong the proceedings and consume needless time. Therefore, it is not because of what appeared in the papers today that I am going to make my remarks as briefly as I possibly can.
At the outset I would like to state my appreciation to the minister and his officials of the courtesy and dispatch with which my representations have been dealt from time to time. When I have had occasion to make representations to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration I have always found the officials extremely co-operative and courteous and I wish to place my appreciation on the record at this point.
I want to speak very briefly with regard to the subject under discussion, immigration.
I feel that immigration should be accelerated.
I am not pleading tonight for a wide-open policy but I think there are some substantial reasons why the inflow of immigrants should be accelerated and this can be done without causing dislocation in our economy to any great extent.
It would seem to me that one reason we should have an increase in the immigration rate is because of the necessity for domestic markets for our products. In a country such as ours, with a population of approximately 16 million, we can readily understand that our costs are high because of the limited market we have. From time to time we have been told that if we had a larger domestic market the prices would go down on Canadian products. I think that is one valid reason why we should set our sights on an increase in the flow of immigrants and should encourage those who are suitable to come to our country.
Another reason I would like to suggest tonight relates to defence. With our vast areas and long borders we can readily understand how serious a situation would confront us in the event of war with the limited manpower we have in Canada. I would suggest that is another valid reason for increasing immigration into Canada.

There is another reason and it is this. In view of the vast size of our country and the relatively small population we have it would seem to me, looking at it from a Christian point of view, that we in this great country ought to be willing to share it with those who are less fortunate and are anxious to make their homes here.
There is perhaps one more reason. It may be that circumstances will force us in the near future to recognize the necessity of opening our doors to more immigrants. I do not think we can forever keep to ourselves this wonderful country of ours. If we are not willing to open the doors a little and accept people into our country to a greater extent than we are at the present time, then it is possible the day will arrive when someone will seize the opportunity of moving, despite our attitude toward their doing so.
For the reasons I have mentioned I would suggest that immigration be stepped up not to the extent, as I say, that it would dislocate our economy but in an orderly fashion that would build up our population as well as provide homes for those who desire to take up residence in Canada.
Earlier in this debate a question was raised concerning not giving a reason to those who are denied entry into Canada or permanent residence here. I believe this causes uneasiness on the part of a great many people who would otherwise want to spend the rest of their lives here in Canada.
Just the other day I had several visitors, some of whom were taking the civil defence course at Arnprior. One man approached me and, referring to a certain case, wanted to know why that person had been denied the privilege of remaining in Canada. I had not heard of the incident and I told him that I did not know. He said that no doubt there must be a reason and he felt that if that man could be ordered out of the country without any reason being given then perhaps he might be the next on the list, that they might come along and tell him that he could not stay in Canada and yet give him no reason. He contended that the reason for such action should be given.
My main reason for rising on this occasion is to speak on behalf of Canadian citizens of East Indian origin. This matter has been referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver East and what I say now I say on behalf of the members from British Columbia who belong to this particular group. In that way we hope to curtail the debate somewhat. This matter has been referred to and broached on a number of occasions but was brought
